name: Public International Law

exam.label: Mon 30 Nov · 09:00–12:00 · USC Hall 2
exam.rules: Closed book, typed on a university Chromebook with no internet. Only a clean hardcopy of Blackstone's International Law Documents (16th ed.) is allowed. Covers all weeks, 1–11 (the syllabus said 7–11; you confirmed the final covers everything). Know the cases and apply them; paragraph numbers are not needed.
exam.format: Expect a layered fictional fact pattern asking you to advise a State (or clerk for an ICJ judge), in the style of the course's sample questions: Azargh and Rio del Oro (weeks 2 and 4), Jalapenia, Assad in Berlin, the EU raw-materials mock, Valdoria/Ironwatch (weeks 7–10). Answer in dependency order: who is the actor (State, people, IO) → which source binds (treaty, custom) → is it valid, in force, reserved, interpreted how → was it breached and attributable → excuses → consequences and invocation.
template: Heading and a one-line bottom line: 'Memorandum to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of X. In short: …'
Issue map, numbered as questions in dependency order. Split your words in proportion to the points per sub-question.

Each issue in IRAC: rule with its source (Blackstone article number plus the case), application using every fact given, the other side's best argument and your rebuttal, mini-conclusion. Marks come in 1–2 point units per correct proposition, so state each step in its own sentence.
If a treaty route fails (non-party, termination, reservation), ask whether a customary rule with the same content still binds (VCLT Art 43; Nicaragua paras 175–179).
Remedies and next steps: cessation, reparation, countermeasures, forum (ICJ jurisdiction).
One or two sentences of critical reflection for originality marks (Eurocentrism, judicial activism in custom-finding, fragmentation).

Tab Blackstone: UN Charter (Arts 1, 2, 4, 25, 39–51, 103), ICJ Statute (Arts 36, 38, 59), VCLT (Arts 2, 7, 11–21, 26–27, 31–33, 34–38, 42–64), Montevideo Convention, GA Res 1514, 1541, 2625, 3314, ARSIWA, Rome Statute, UNCSI.

topics.title: International law as a discipline
core: Definition (Restatement 3rd, 1987): the law concerned with the conduct of States and international organisations and their relations inter se, and some of their relations with natural and legal persons.

A horizontal system: no central legislator, executive or compulsory court; its subjects make the law (treaty, custom). Yet not fully equal: permanent membership and the veto (Charter Arts 23, 27(3)) — 'all States are equal, but some are more equal than others'.

'Is it law?' objections: Austin (no sovereign command, no sanction); realists (Morgenthau, Aron: law 'merely ratifies the fate of arms'); Hart (primary rules without full secondary rules of recognition, change and adjudication).

Replies: States treat it as law and argue in its terms; sanctions exist in other forms (nullity, non-opposability, responsibility, countermeasures); high compliance (Henkin: 'almost all nations observe almost all principles … almost all of the time').
Voluntarism: Lotus (1927) — 'rules of law binding upon States … emanate from their own free will'. Qualified by jus cogens, erga omnes obligations, and custom binding new States.
Is it 'international'? Roberts: the field is dominated by a few Western States' practitioners, cases and textbooks.

Koskenniemi, 'Histories of International Law: Dealing with Eurocentrism' (compulsory): histories told from Europe (Westphalia, Vitoria, Grotius) as progress; postcolonial critique (Anghie: built through the colonial encounter and the civilising mission), yet the colonised used the same tools (sovereignty, self-determination). Ways to deal with Eurocentrism: colonial origins of rules, the colonial encounter as foundational, hybridisation and agency, 'provincialising' Europe.

Doctrinal traces of Eurocentrism: 'civilized nations' in ICJ Statute Art 38(1)(c); Island of Palmas treating agreements with native chiefs as non-treaties; Western Sahara (Bilad Chinguitti lacked personality); uti possidetis freezing colonial borders.
Pauwelyn, Wessel and Wouters (recommended): formal treaty-making stagnates while informal law-making (networks, standards, MOUs) grows.

Monism and dualism (Hernández ch 4). Monism (Kelsen's single Grundnorm; Lauterpacht placing international law at the apex): treaties apply without transformation (France, Spain, Germany, the Netherlands). Dualism (the UK, the US, Scandinavia): a treaty is not part of domestic law until enacted (Thomas v Baptiste, PC 1999; JH Rayner v DTI, HL 1989: treaties 'are not self-executing'). Custom is generally part of domestic law in both kinds of system (Trendtex 1977; Paquete Habana 1900). Fitzmaurice and Rousseau's coordination view: each order is supreme in its field, and conflicts are handled through State responsibility, not invalidity. Hernández: the debate shows 'fatigue', and one should not reduce dualism to legal nationalism or praise monism as 'courageous committed internationalism'.

On the international plane, international law prevails: internal law is no excuse (ARSIWA Art 3; VCLT Art 27; Alabama Claims), but the domestic act is not void; the State is responsible. LaGrand and Avena (US procedural default) and Medellín v Texas (US Sup Ct 2008: Avena not directly enforceable federal law) show the gap. Legislation can itself breach international law where it is designed to be applied (Nicaragua v Colombia 2022 para 194: bring Decree 1946 into conformity). International courts treat municipal law as fact (Upper Silesia) and defer to national courts' reading of their own law (Serbian Loans) unless it is manifestly incorrect (Diallo 2010).

Hernández's own answer to 'is it law?': it is 'too simplistic' to deny that international law is law because it is institutionally deficient. It has the 'seeds' of a legal system (recognised sources, legal persons, rules of interpretation applied by impartial third parties, responsibility for breach, even a hierarchy of norms) and an 'invisible college' of lawyers sharing a vocabulary; Crawford: it provides 'not merely the vocabulary of inter-State relations but its underlying grammar'. Its basis is consent, reciprocity and good faith (Charter Art 2(2)), challenged by Verdross and Simma's 'formless consensus' and Peters' 'humanization'. It grows by 'sedimentation', not revolution.
lecture: Lecture 1 (Marhold) asks three questions: what is international law (Restatement definition); is it a European invention (jus gentium versus 'law among nations', 'international law' as Bentham's coinage); is it really law?

The domestic-law analogy diagram: vertical national systems (legislature, executive, courts over individuals) versus horizontal PIL between States. Charter Art 23 illustrates hierarchy within formal equality.

The three challenges taught: the domestic analogy (law as coercive command), classical realism ('international law can merely ratify the fate of arms and the arbitration of force'), and Hart's analytical theory (primary versus secondary rules).

cases.name: SS Lotus (France v Turkey)
cases.holding: Rules binding States emanate from their own free will; restrictions on independence cannot be presumed.
cases.use: The voluntarist baseline (and its critique).

cases.name: Island of Palmas (Netherlands v US)
cases.holding: Sovereignty means independence, the exclusive right to exercise State functions over territory; title requires continuous and peaceful display of sovereignty. Agreements with native princes were not treaties.
cases.use: Sovereignty; intertemporal law; Eurocentrism critique.

cards.q: What are the three classic objections to the legal character of international law?
cards.a: Austin: no sovereign command backed by sanction. Realists (Morgenthau, Aron): law merely ratifies power. Hart: a set of primary rules lacking full secondary rules of recognition, change and adjudication.

cards.q: Give two doctrinal traces of Eurocentrism the course points to.
cards.a: 'Civilized nations' in ICJ Statute Art 38(1)(c) (introduced by Descamps); Island of Palmas treating agreements with native chiefs as non-treaties; Western Sahara and the Bilad Chinguitti; uti possidetis freezing colonial borders.

cards.q: Henkin's compliance line?
cards.a: 'Almost all nations observe almost all principles of international law and almost all of their obligations almost all of the time.'

cards.q: A ratified but unincorporated treaty: can a UK court apply it, and can a Dutch court?
cards.a: UK (dualist): no direct effect until Parliament enacts it (Thomas v Baptiste; JH Rayner), though courts may use it to interpret statutes. Netherlands (monist): treaty provisions that are binding on everyone by their content apply once published and prevail over conflicting statutes (Dutch Constitution Arts 93–94). Either way the State remains internationally responsible for a breach (VCLT Art 27; ARSIWA Art 3).

excerpts.source: SS Lotus (France v Turkey)
excerpts.text: International law governs relations between independent States. The rules of law binding upon States therefore emanate from their own free will as expressed in conventions or by usages generally accepted as expressing principles of law… Restrictions upon the independence of States cannot therefore be presumed.
excerpts.why: The voluntarist, consent-based picture of IL that later doctrine (and Week 1) pushes back against.

topics.title: States and peoples
core: Statehood criteria (Montevideo Art 1, reflecting custom): permanent population (no minimum); defined territory (borders need not be settled — North Sea para 46); effective government (strict at birth, loose for existing States; Tinoco: a de facto government binds the State); capacity to enter into relations, i.e. independence (puppet States fail: Manchukuo, TRNC).

Additional legality requirement: an entity created through unlawful force or in breach of self-determination or jus cogens is not accepted (SC Res 216/217 Southern Rhodesia, 541 TRNC; Kosovo para 81). Democracy and human rights as emerging criteria (EC Guidelines 1991) remain unsettled.

Territory: title by treaty or agreement; uti possidetis juris turns colonial administrative lines into international borders (Burkina Faso/Mali para 23); title prevails over effectivités, which matter only where no title exists. Presumption of continuity: losing an element (e.g. land to sea-level rise) does not necessarily end statehood (Climate AO 2025 para 363).

Recognition: declaratory theory dominant (Montevideo Art 3; Badinter Opinion 1) versus constitutive (Oppenheim). Recognition is strong evidence when criteria are doubtful (Kosovo, Palestine); premature recognition can be unlawful intervention; duty of non-recognition for serious breaches of peremptory norms (Namibia, Wall, OPT 2024; ARSIWA Art 41(2)).

Treaty-specific (functional) statehood: ICC PTC I (5 Feb 2021) treated Palestine as a 'State' for the Rome Statute after its accession without deciding general statehood. A useful counsel move when general statehood is doubtful.

Sovereignty: independence and exclusive State functions over territory (Island of Palmas); sovereign equality (Charter Art 2(1); Res 2625); non-intervention between States, a customary rule (Nicaragua paras 202–205; Res 2625); Art 2(7) itself only bars the UN from intervening in matters of domestic jurisdiction.

Self-determination: Charter Arts 1(2), 55; common Art 1 ICCPR/ICESCR; Res 1514 (declaratory of custom by 1965 — Chagos paras 150–153); Res 1541 (independence, free association or integration); Res 2625 (saving clause for States with a government representing the whole people).

Who is a 'people'? Clearly colonial peoples, peoples under alien subjugation, domination or exploitation, and under foreign occupation (Kosovo para 79; OPT 2024, where self-determination is peremptory, para 233). Contested: minorities inside existing States.

Internal (participation, autonomy) versus external self-determination (independence). External only clearly for colonial and occupied peoples; otherwise it clashes with territorial integrity and uti possidetis. Remedial secession is contested (Quebec Reference obiter; ICJ declined in Kosovo paras 82–83).

Kosovo AO (2010): no prohibition of declarations of independence in general IL (para 84); territorial integrity applies between States (para 80); prior illegal declarations were illegal because of force or jus cogens breaches (para 81). It said nothing on statehood or a right to secede.

Badinter Commission: Opinion 1 (statehood by usual criteria; recognition declaratory; SFRY in dissolution — dissolution differs from secession, so no parent consent needed and assets and debts are shared); Opinion 2 (self-determination cannot change existing frontiers except by agreement; minorities' rights, arguably overstated as peremptory); Opinion 3 (uti possidetis applied outside the colonial context).

Palestine at the ICC: Appeals Chamber 24 Apr 2025 remanded Israel's Art 19(2) challenge (Oslo, statehood) and 15 Dec 2025 (3–2) upheld rejection of Israel's Art 18(1) request. The jurisdiction challenge on remand is pending (no ruling found by Nov 2026), and the warrants stay in force (PTC I, July 2025).

Recognition wave (Sept 2025): the UK, Canada, Australia and Portugal (21 Sept) and France, Belgium, Luxembourg, Malta, Monaco and Andorra (22 Sept) recognised Palestine, bringing the total to about 157 of 193 UN members. The GA endorsed the New York Declaration on the two-State solution (142–10–12, 12 Sept 2025). On the declaratory view, recognition is evidence that the criteria are met (or are relaxed for a people with a right to self-determination under occupation, OPT AO 2024 para 233). On the constitutive view, it adds to Palestine's statehood. Not UN membership (SC veto).

Chagos follow-up: the UK–Mauritius treaty (signed 22 May 2025: sovereignty to Mauritius, 99-year lease of Diego Garcia) had still not entered into force by Oct 2026. The UK implementing bill stalled after US opposition (Feb 2026), and Mauritius is considering litigation. Teaching point: decolonisation remains incomplete (Chagos AO 2019, Res 1514 para 6) and a signed but unratified treaty does not bind (VCLT Arts 14, 18).

Effective government at birth can be relaxed through collective recognition or UN admission: Zaire (1960), Guinea-Bissau, and Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina (EC recognition 1992, then UN admission) despite lacking control of much of their territory. Hernández: collective recognition 'cured' the defects, and the two theories coexist. The declaratory theory cannot explain the effect of refusals to recognise; the constitutive theory explains collective recognition but gives a political act legal weight. Lauterpacht's duty to recognise remains a minority view. Contrast the Åland Islands report (1920): Finland was not 'definitely constituted' until its authorities could assert themselves without foreign troops.

Recognition of governments is distinct from recognition of States: a coup does not affect the State's identity. De jure recognition needs effective control 'with a reasonable prospect of permanence'; de facto recognition signals doubts about legitimacy (UK–USSR 1921 de facto, 1924 de jure). A government recognised only de facto cannot claim State property or invoke immunity in the recognising State's courts. The US (1977) and UK (1980) stopped formally recognising governments; UK courts apply Somalia v Woodhouse Drake (1993): administrative control, dealings with the UK government, and international recognition in marginal cases. De jure recognition has returned as a policy tool: Libya's NTC (July 2011, before it controlled Tripoli), Venezuela (Guaidó 2019, González 2024), the Taliban (no formal recognition when the book was written, though China accepted a Taliban ambassador in Jan 2024; Russia formally recognised the Taliban government in July 2025, which postdates the book) and Myanmar.
lecture: Lecture 2 opens with an 'old debate': the Valladolid controversy between Sepúlveda and Las Casas (1550) on the status of indigenous political entities.

'Subject of international law' is a descriptive, doctrinal concept, not a legal term of art. Three approaches to identifying subjects, including the purely European perspective (the Bilad Chinguitti in Western Sahara) and the ICJ's functional approach in Reparation.
Summary slide: States have absolute personality and peoples the right to self-determination; States make international law.

cases.name: Frontier Dispute (Burkina Faso/Mali)
cases.holding: Uti possidetis juris is a general principle aimed at stability: colonial administrative boundaries become international frontiers on independence. Title prevails over effectivités.
cases.use: Territory; borders in secession and dissolution.

cases.name: Accordance with IL of Kosovo's Declaration of Independence
cases.holding: General IL contains no prohibition of declarations of independence; territorial integrity governs inter-State relations; SC Res 1244 did not bar the declaration, whose authors acted outside the interim framework.
cases.use: Secession questions; the limits of the AO.

cases.name: Chagos Archipelago AO
cases.holding: Res 1514 reflected custom by 1965; detachment of Chagos without the free and genuine will of the people meant decolonisation was not lawfully completed; the UK must end its administration as rapidly as possible; erga omnes, all States must cooperate.
cases.use: Self-determination as custom; GA resolutions as evidence; erga omnes.

cases.name: Legal Consequences of Israel's Policies in the OPT AO
cases.holding: Self-determination is peremptory in situations of foreign occupation; Israel's policies amount to annexation; its presence is unlawful; non-recognition and non-assistance duties for all States.
cases.use: Peoples under occupation; Art 41 consequences.

cases.name: Reference re Secession of Quebec
cases.holding: No right to unilateral secession under domestic or international law for a people enjoying internal self-determination; external self-determination arises for colonial or oppressed peoples (remedial secession left open).
cases.use: Internal versus external self-determination.

cases.name: Tinoco Arbitration (UK v Costa Rica)
cases.holding: A de facto government in effective control binds the State, even if unrecognised by others.
cases.use: Effective government; recognition's evidentiary role.

cases.name: Situation in Palestine (Art 19(3) decision)
cases.holding: Palestine is a State Party; for Art 12(2)(a) it is the State on whose territory conduct occurred, covering Gaza and the West Bank including East Jerusalem. Judge Kovács dissented in part (Oslo Accords).
cases.use: Treaty-specific statehood.

cases.name: Åland Islands (Report of the International Committee of Jurists)
cases.court: League of Nations, Committee of Jurists
cases.holding: The League was competent over the dispute. Finland, which declared independence in 1917, 'had not yet acquired the status of a definitely constituted State' until a stable political organisation existed and the public authorities could assert themselves throughout the territory without the help of foreign troops. Sovereignty was later confirmed for Finland, with minority guarantees and demilitarisation.
cases.use: Effective government as a condition of statehood at birth; self-determination of a minority did not override sovereignty.

cards.q: What are the four Montevideo criteria, and how strict is each?
cards.a: Permanent population (no minimum); defined territory (borders need not be settled); effective government (strict at birth, loose for existing States); capacity to enter into relations = independence (puppets fail). Plus a legality requirement: no creation by unlawful force or breach of self-determination.

cards.q: Declaratory versus constitutive recognition?
cards.a: Declaratory (dominant; Montevideo Art 3; Badinter Opinion 1): statehood exists once the criteria are met, recognition acknowledges it. Constitutive (Oppenheim): recognition creates the State. In practice recognition is strong evidence where criteria are doubtful.

cards.q: What is the model-answer chain for a secession question (Azargh)?
cards.a: (1) Legal basis (common Art 1 Covenants, Res 1514, 1541, 2625); (2) no definition of 'people' — apply the facts; (3) internal versus external; (4) external only for colonial and occupied peoples (Kosovo, Chagos); (5) otherwise uti possidetis and territorial integrity; (6) a declaration itself is not prohibited (Kosovo); (7) statehood outside decolonisation needs the parent State's consent (Badinter, Quebec); (8) remedial secession as a contested extra; (9) conclusion.

cards.q: Dissolution versus secession (Badinter)?
cards.a: Dissolution: the parent State disappears and all units are successors on an equal footing; no parent consent needed; assets, debts and treaties are shared. Secession: the parent continues and its consent matters.

cards.q: What did Chagos say about GA Res 1514 and custom?
cards.a: Adopted 89–0–9 with no State disputing it, clear normative wording and consistent decolonisation practice, it was declaratory of custom by 1965 (paras 150–153). Territorial integrity of the whole non-self-governing territory is a corollary (para 160).

cards.q: Name the 'treaty-specific statehood' technique and its source.
cards.a: ICC PTC I (2021, Palestine): asking whether an entity is a 'State' for the purposes of a particular treaty after its accession, rather than deciding general statehood. Supported by the Heinsch and Pinzauti amicus (effet utile, ASP practice, acquiescence, occupation not defeating statehood).

cards.q: How would a court decide whether an entity is the government of a State, now that the UK no longer recognises governments?
cards.a: Somalia v Woodhouse Drake (1993): whether it is the constitutional government; the degree and nature of its administrative control over the territory; the UK government's dealings with it; and, in marginal cases, its international recognition. Internationally, de jure recognition requires effective control with a reasonable prospect of permanence and independence from foreign control (contrast Libya's NTC, 2011).

excerpts.source: Montevideo Convention on the Rights and Duties of States (1933)
excerpts.text: The state as a person of international law should possess the following qualifications: (a) a permanent population; (b) a defined territory; (c) government; and (d) capacity to enter into relations with other states.
excerpts.why: The starting point for any statehood problem; then test effectiveness, legality (Res 2625, 1514) and recognition.

excerpts.source: Accordance with IL of the Unilateral Declaration of Independence in respect of Kosovo
excerpts.text: …the Court considers that general international law contains no applicable prohibition of declarations of independence. Accordingly, it concludes that the declaration of independence of 17 February 2008 did not violate general international law.
excerpts.why: A narrow answer: a declaration is not unlawful as such, but the Court said nothing on remedial secession or on whether Kosovo is a State.

topics.title: Non-state actors: IOs, individuals, corporations
core: Personality is not all-or-nothing (Reparation 1949): 'the subjects of law in any legal system are not necessarily identical in their nature or in the extent of their rights, and their nature depends upon the needs of the community'.

IO definition: ARIO Art 2(a) (established by treaty or other instrument governed by IL, with its own legal personality); Schermers & Blokker (an international agreement, at least one organ with a will of its own, established under IL); VCLT Art 2(1)(i) 'intergovernmental organization'.

Reparation: the UN's personality was inferred from its functions, organs, privileges and immunities (Art 105), treaty-making (Art 43) and members' obligations (Art 2(5)) — capacity to bring claims, including functional protection of agents (Bernadotte). 'Not the same thing as saying that it is a State … or a super-State.'

Objective personality: 50 States representing the vast majority could create an entity with personality opposable to non-members (Reparation), in tension with VCLT Art 34; applied to the ICC by PTC I (Bangladesh/Myanmar 2018, para 48).

Principle of speciality (WHO Nuclear Weapons AO 1996, para 25): IOs lack general competence. The WHO could ask about health effects, not legality of use, which belongs to the UN security organs — the third condition of Art 96(2) (within the scope of activities) failed.

Implied powers: powers 'conferred by necessary implication as being essential to the performance of its duties' (Reparation); Certain Expenses (1962): action appropriate to a stated purpose is presumed intra vires. Constituent instruments are treaties 'of a particular type' (WHO AO para 19): effectiveness and the organisation's practice weigh heavily (Namibia 1971: abstention is not a veto under Art 27(3)).

IOs are bound by general IL, their constitutions and their agreements (WHO–Egypt AO 1980 para 37); 1986 VCLT for their treaties; ARIO 2011 for responsibility. IO practice can contribute to custom (ILC Conclusion 4(2)).

Individuals: no general law-making or claim capacity, but rights under customary human rights law and duties under ICL (IMT: 'crimes … are committed by men, not by abstract entities'). Treaties can confer rights directly if intended (Danzig Railway Officials 1928; LaGrand 2001 para 77 on VCCR Art 36). Procedural capacity where a treaty gives it (ECtHR, IACtHR, investor–State arbitration). Cançado Trindade (Germany v Italy, separate opinion to the 2011 Order on Greece's intervention, para 34): individuals are true subjects. (In the 2012 merits judgment he dissented.)

Corporations: no general personality; they act through domestic law and treaties granting standing (BITs, ICSID). UNGPs (2011): Pillar I State duty to protect (legal), Pillar II corporate responsibility to respect through human rights due diligence (social expectation), Pillar III access to remedy. OECD Guidelines (2023): soft law with National Contact Points. CESCR General Comment 24 (2017): States must regulate companies domiciled in their territory, including conduct abroad.

Special cases: Holy See, Sovereign Order of Malta, insurgents and belligerents (limited personality under IHL), national liberation movements (API Art 1(4)). ILA Non-State Actors Committee (2016): involving NSAs without giving them State-like status.

Theories of IO personality: functionalist (implied from the functions and powers conferred), will theory (personality exists if the members intended it, inferred from the powers given) and objective (personality follows automatically once objective criteria are met, such as an organ with a will distinct from the members'). International personality does not automatically bring domestic personality: Charter Art 104 obliges members to grant it; monist States give effect on ratification, dualist ones by statute; non-members may recognise it through comity (Arab Monetary Fund v Hashim, HL 1991). Members are presumed not liable for the IO's debts (International Tin Council litigation; JH Rayner v DTI, HL 1989).

Attribution between an IO and its members (ARIO): the conduct of the IO's organs and agents acting in the performance of their functions belongs to the IO (Art 6). For State organs lent to an IO, such as peacekeepers, the test is effective control over the specific conduct (Art 7). The ECtHR in Behrami & Saramati (2007) used 'ultimate authority and control' to attribute KFOR/UNMIK conduct to the UN and declared the case inadmissible; Hernández calls this 'untenable' because States keep command yet escape liability. Al-Jedda (2011): the UK was responsible in Iraq. Nuhanović and Mustafić (Dutch Supreme Court 2013): Dutchbat's conduct at Srebrenica was attributable to the Netherlands, and dual attribution is possible. An IO may not circumvent its obligations by binding or authorising members (ARIO Art 17), and members may not hide behind the IO (Art 61). ARIO are criticised as one-size-fits-all, modelled too closely on ARSIWA, and thin on practice.

Review of SC decisions: the ICJ has no power of judicial review (Namibia 1971, though it checked that Res 276 was adopted in conformity with the Charter). Regional courts review implementing measures: Kadi (CJEU 2008; Kadi II 2013: targeted sanctions breached fundamental rights for lack of evidence) and Nada v Switzerland (ECtHR GC 2012). Judge ad hoc Lauterpacht (Bosnia Genocide, provisional measures 1993): Art 103 cannot extend to a conflict between an SC resolution and jus cogens.
lecture: Lecture 3 contrasts individuals and States: under general IL individuals have no capacity to operate on the international plane, make law or bring claims, but hold customary human rights and criminal accountability; under lex specialis they gain substantive rights (human rights and investment treaties) and procedural rights (regional courts, investor–State arbitration).
Cançado Trindade's separate opinion in Germany v Italy (2011 Order, Greece intervening, para 34) is quoted on individuals as subjects.
'Objective' personality is tested against VCLT Art 34, Reparation, the ICC PTC I decision of 2018 (para 48) and Crawford's view (Brownlie, 9th edn, p 160).
IOs on the international plane: what rules bind them (WHO–Egypt para 37), and the distinction between the international plane and domestic legal orders.

cases.name: Reparation for Injuries (AO)
cases.holding: The UN has international personality and capacity to bring claims, including for injury to its agents (functional protection), even against a non-member, inferred from its functions and implied powers.
cases.use: IO personality; implied powers; objective personality.

cases.name: Legality of the Use of Nuclear Weapons (WHO request)
cases.holding: The WHO's request fell outside the scope of its activities: IOs are governed by the principle of speciality; legality of use belongs to the UN.
cases.use: Speciality; Art 96(2) conditions.

cases.name: LaGrand (Germany v US)
cases.holding: VCCR Art 36(1) creates individual rights, which the national State may invoke.
cases.use: Individual rights under treaties.

cases.name: Bangladesh/Myanmar (Art 19(3) decision)
cases.holding: The ICC has objective international legal personality (para 48), drawing on Reparation; jurisdiction where part of a crime (deportation) occurred on a State Party's territory.
cases.use: Objective personality; territorial jurisdiction.

cases.name: Netherlands v Nuhanović (and Mustafić)
cases.court: Supreme Court of the Netherlands (Hoge Raad)
cases.holding: The Netherlands was responsible for Dutchbat's handing over of Bosnian Muslim men from the Srebrenica compound in July 1995. Applying effective control (ARIO Art 7, ARSIWA Art 8), conduct can be attributed to more than one actor; that the UN had command did not exclude attribution to the Netherlands, which in fact controlled the evacuation.
cases.use: Dual attribution in peace operations; contrast Behrami & Saramati (ECtHR 2007, 'ultimate authority and control' → UN).

cards.q: Three conditions for a specialised agency's advisory-opinion request (Art 96(2))?
cards.a: Authorised organ; a legal question; arising within the scope of its activities. The WHO's 1996 request failed the third (speciality).

cards.q: How did the ICJ find UN personality in Reparation?
cards.a: Not from an express provision, but by inference from its functions and the rights it was intended to exercise: organs, tasks, privileges and immunities (Art 105), treaty-making (Art 43), members' duties (Art 2(5)). Personality is functional, not State-like.

cards.q: Is a corporation bound by human rights treaties?
cards.a: Not directly. Argue via the home or host State's duty to protect (UNGP Pillar I, CESCR GC 24, extraterritorial regulation), soft-law expectations on the company (UNGP Pillar II, OECD Guidelines), and any BIT the company may invoke against the State.

cards.q: What is objective international personality, and why is it controversial?
cards.a: Personality opposable to non-members, as the ICJ held for the UN (50 States representing the vast majority) and ICC PTC I for the ICC (2018). Controversial because it sits uneasily with pacta tertiis (VCLT Art 34).

cards.q: Peacekeepers lent to the UN commit a wrongful act: who is responsible?
cards.a: Whoever had effective control over the specific conduct (ARIO Art 7), and possibly both (dual attribution, Nuhanović 2013). The ECtHR's 'ultimate authority and control' test in Behrami & Saramati (2007) attributed the conduct to the UN alone; Al-Jedda (2011) distinguished it and held the UK responsible in Iraq. Hernández criticises Behrami because troop contributors keep national command but escape liability.

excerpts.source: Reparation for Injuries Suffered in the Service of the United Nations
excerpts.text: …the Organization is an international person. That is not the same thing as saying that it is a State, which it certainly is not, or that its legal personality and rights and duties are the same as those of a State.
excerpts.why: Objective personality of the UN, derived from its functions; the basis for implied powers.

excerpts.source: Legality of the Use by a State of Nuclear Weapons in Armed Conflict (WHO request)
excerpts.text: International organizations are governed by the 'principle of speciality', that is to say, they are invested by the States which create them with powers, the limits of which are a function of the common interests whose promotion those States entrust to them.
excerpts.why: The limit on implied powers: the WHO could not ask about legality of use, only health effects.

topics.title: The law of treaties
core: Scope (VCLT Arts 1–2(1)(a)): an agreement between States, in writing, governed by IL, 'whatever its particular designation'. The test is intent to be bound, read from text and circumstances (Qatar v Bahrain: Doha Minutes; Somalia v Kenya: MOU). Non-registration (Charter Art 102) does not affect validity. The VCLT is residual; excludes agreements with IOs (Art 3), succession, responsibility, hostilities (Art 73); non-retroactive (Art 4), but most of it reflects custom.

Who binds the State (Art 7): full powers, or ex officio Heads of State and Government and Foreign Ministers; heads of mission for adopting texts; other ministers may bind in their field (DRC v Rwanda para 47). Consent (Arts 11–15); entry into force (Art 24); Art 18 obligation not to defeat object and purpose before entry into force.

Internal law: Art 27 no excuse; Art 46 invalidity only if the violation of internal competence rules is manifest and of fundamental importance (Cameroon v Nigeria; Somalia v Kenya paras 48–49). Acquiescence bars relative invalidity grounds (Art 45).

Reservations (Arts 2(1)(d), 19–23; ILC Guide to Practice 2011): label irrelevant; interpretative declarations that modify effect are reservations (Belilos). Permissible unless prohibited, outside permitted categories, or contrary to object and purpose (Art 19; Genocide Reservations AO 1951). Tacit acceptance after 12 months (Art 20(5)). Effects (Art 21): accepted → modified reciprocally (Art 21(1)); simple objection → the provision does not apply to the extent of the reservation (Art 21(3)); maximum-effect objection → no treaty relations (Art 20(4)(b)). Invalid reservation: party without the benefit unless it shows it would not be bound (Guide 4.5.3); human rights bodies sever (Belilos, Loizidou, HRC GC 24).

DRC v Rwanda (2006): a reservation to Art IX of the Genocide Convention is not contrary to object and purpose; jus cogens does not itself confer jurisdiction. Joint Separate Opinion (Higgins, Kooijmans, Elaraby, Owada, Simma): the 1951 consent-based model is ill-suited to human rights treaties; courts now rule on compatibility; reservations to monitoring clauses may defeat object and purpose.
Third States (Arts 34–38): no obligations without express written consent (Art 35); rights presumed accepted (Art 36); a treaty rule may bind third States as custom (Art 38).

Interpretation (Arts 31–33): one integrated rule — good faith, ordinary meaning, context, object and purpose, subsequent agreements and practice (31(3)(a)–(b)), relevant rules of IL between the parties (31(3)(c)); supplementary means to confirm or resolve ambiguity (Art 32). Costa Rica v Nicaragua (2009): no restrictive interpretation of sovereignty limits (para 48); generic terms in treaties of unlimited duration are presumed to evolve (para 66: 'comercio' covers passenger transport). Ukraine v Russia (2024, ICSFT) paras 42–53: 'funds' means assets provided for their monetary value, not weapons or training. IACtHR OC-23/17 paras 40–45: living instrument, pro persona, Art 31(3)(c) bringing in environmental law.

Pauwelyn and Elsig: interpretation is political — dominant hermeneutic (text, intent, teleology), timing (original versus evolutive), activism, precedent, linkage; choices depend on interpretation space and incentives (institutional design). The ICJ evolves only where parties used generic terms in long-term treaties; human rights courts evolve from object and purpose.

Invalidity: relative (Arts 46–50: internal law, authority, error, fraud, corruption); absolute (51 coercion of a representative, 52 coercion by force, 53 jus cogens, void ab initio; 64 new jus cogens terminates).

Termination and suspension: by the treaty or consent (54, 57); denunciation without a clause only if intended or implied (56, 12 months' notice); material breach (60; not for humanitarian provisions, 60(5)); supervening impossibility (61); fundamental change of circumstances (62; not boundary treaties, not self-induced); procedure (65–67); custom survives (Art 43).

Gabčíkovo-Nagymaros (1997): necessity does not terminate a treaty, it only excuses non-performance (paras 47–48, 101); impossibility, fundamental change and material breach all rejected (paras 103–110); new environmental norms enter through the treaty's evolving provisions (paras 111–114); the treaty remains in force and the parties must negotiate in good faith.

Impermissible reservations, two schools: permissibility (validity is an objective question of compatibility with object and purpose; acceptance cannot cure it; the reservation can be severed) and opposability (validity depends on other parties' acceptance). Practice: when the Maldives acceded to CEDAW (1993) with Sharia and constitution reservations, Austria and Portugal objected but kept treaty relations (permissibility), while Sweden treated its consent as invalid (opposability). Human rights bodies sever: Belilos, Loizidou (Turkey bound despite its intention), Hilaire v Trinidad and Tobago (IACtHR 2001), HRC GC 24 and Rawle Kennedy (1999), after which Trinidad and Tobago denounced the First Optional Protocol. The 2007 meeting of the ILC and human rights bodies endorsed a 'reservations dialogue'.

Interpretation fine points: there is no hierarchy among the Art 31 elements (the ILC's 'crucible'; Koskenniemi: Art 31 lists 'virtually all thinkable interpretative methods'). Subsequent practice is read restrictively: Kasikili/Sedudu (1999) excluded one party's internal acts, and Whaling (2014) refused to treat IWC resolutions not supported by all parties as Art 31(3)(b) practice. Art 31(3)(c) was used in Oil Platforms (Charter on force) and Djibouti v France (2008), but Certain Iranian Assets (2019) refused to read customary immunities into the Treaty of Amity. The principle of effectiveness cannot override clear text and intent (Interpretation of Peace Treaties, 1950). Travaux are now routinely examined to confirm a reading (Georgia v Russia 2011; Qatar v UAE 2021).

Material breach and fundamental change, fine print. Art 60(3): a material breach is an unlawful repudiation or the violation of a provision essential to the object and purpose; it is rarely invoked (the OIC's 1979 suspension of Egypt). In a multilateral treaty, one party's breach does not excuse another towards non-breaching parties, and Art 60(5) protects only humanitarian treaties (Hernández regrets that environmental and disarmament treaties are left out). Fundamental change: Fisheries Jurisdiction (UK v Iceland, 1973) requires a radical transformation of the obligations still to be performed; only the ECJ in Racke (1998, the Yugoslav civil war) has ever upheld the plea. Supervening impossibility needs the permanent disappearance of an indispensable object (e.g. a river drying up) not caused by the invoking party.
lecture: Lecture 4 (Marhold) frames two basic principles of the VCLT: safeguarding sovereignty (freedom to opt out of its rules, reservations, consent) and restricting sovereignty for the common interest (pacta sunt servanda Art 26, Art 18, jus cogens).

A slide contrasts treaty law (conditions for lawfully denouncing or suspending treaties) with State responsibility (grounds precluding wrongfulness) — the Gabčíkovo separation, a classic exam link to weeks 10–11.
Qatar v Bahrain and Somalia v Kenya quoted on 'whatever its particular designation'; the VCLT is 'subsidiary in nature', applying only where the treaty has no rule of its own.

cases.name: Maritime Delimitation and Territorial Questions (Qatar v Bahrain)
cases.holding: Signed Minutes enumerating commitments are a treaty; the actual terms and circumstances decide, not a minister's later claim that he did not intend to be bound; non-registration does not affect validity.
cases.use: What is a treaty.

cases.name: Maritime Delimitation in the Indian Ocean (Somalia v Kenya), PO
cases.holding: An MOU signed under full powers, with an entry-into-force-on-signature clause, registered and unprotested for years, is a valid treaty; Somalia's internal-law objection was not manifest (Art 46) and it had acquiesced (Art 45).
cases.use: Form, consent, internal law, acquiescence.

cases.name: Armed Activities (DRC v Rwanda), Jurisdiction
cases.holding: Rwanda's reservation to Art IX of the Genocide Convention is valid; jus cogens and erga omnes do not confer jurisdiction. A minister of justice's statement could in principle bind the State but was not specific enough.
cases.use: Reservations; Art 7; unilateral acts.

cases.name: Navigational and Related Rights (Costa Rica v Nicaragua)
cases.holding: 'Comercio' in an 1858 treaty of unlimited duration is a generic term with an evolving meaning, now covering passenger transport including tourists; no restrictive interpretation in favour of sovereignty.
cases.use: The template interpretation sequence.

cases.name: Ukraine v Russia (ICSFT and CERD)
cases.holding: 'Funds' in ICSFT Art 1(1) refers to resources provided or collected for their monetary and financial value and does not include the means used to commit terrorist acts, so supplying weapons or organising training is not financing under the Convention (para 53).
cases.use: Textual and contextual interpretation narrowing a term.

cases.name: Gabčíkovo-Nagymaros (Hungary/Slovakia)
cases.holding: Hungary's purported termination was ineffective: necessity is not a termination ground; no impossibility, fundamental change or prior material breach; the treaty remains in force.
cases.use: Termination grounds; treaty law versus State responsibility.

cases.name: Reservations to the Genocide Convention (AO)
cases.holding: A reserving State can be a party if its reservation is compatible with the object and purpose; each State judges compatibility for itself.
cases.use: Origin of the object-and-purpose test.

cases.name: Anglo-French Continental Shelf (UK/France)
cases.holding: France had reserved Art 6 of the 1958 Continental Shelf Convention; the UK objected without saying the treaty should not enter into force. A 'simple' objection does not prevent treaty relations: the combined effect was to make Art 6 inapplicable between the two States 'to the extent of the reservations', neither wholly applicable nor wholly inapplicable; custom filled the gap.
cases.use: Effect of a simple objection (VCLT Art 21(3)); a 'hard' objection must be stated expressly.

cases.name: Application of the Interim Accord of 13 September 1995 (FYROM v Greece)
cases.holding: Greece breached the Interim Accord by objecting to FYROM's NATO membership. Its defences of exceptio non adimpleti contractus/material breach and countermeasures failed: FYROM's only breach (a prohibited symbol on its flag in 2004) had ceased when Greece complained, was not material, and was unconnected with Greece's conduct.
cases.use: Treaty-law and State-responsibility responses to breach can be pleaded together but both need a real, serious prior breach; link to Gabčíkovo and to Art 60 versus countermeasures.

cases.name: Fisheries Jurisdiction (UK v Iceland), Jurisdiction
cases.holding: A fundamental change of circumstances may justify termination only if it radically transforms the extent of the obligations still to be performed, increasing their burden so that performance becomes something essentially different from what was undertaken. Iceland's argument from developments in fishing techniques and the law of the sea did not meet that test.
cases.use: The strict rebus sic stantibus test (VCLT Art 62).

cards.q: What makes an instrument a treaty?
cards.a: An agreement between States, in writing, governed by international law, with intent to be bound, whatever its designation (VCLT Art 2(1)(a)). Judged by the actual terms and the circumstances of conclusion (Qatar v Bahrain; Somalia v Kenya).

cards.q: When does a violation of internal law invalidate consent?
cards.a: Only if it is manifest (objectively evident to any State acting in good faith, at least properly publicised) and concerns a rule of fundamental importance (VCLT Art 46; Cameroon v Nigeria; Somalia v Kenya). Otherwise Art 27 applies.

cards.q: Effects of a reservation that is accepted versus objected to?
cards.a: Accepted: the provision is modified for both parties reciprocally (Art 21(1)). Simple objection: the provision does not apply between them to the extent of the reservation (Art 21(3)). Maximum-effect objection: no treaty relations (Art 20(4)(b)).

cards.q: What is the Costa Rica v Nicaragua sequence for interpretation?
cards.a: No restrictive presumption (para 48) → text ambiguous ('con objetos de comercio') → context resolves it (51–56) → contemporaneity argument (58) → reject over-broad reading (59–61) → common intention may be evolving (63–64) → generic terms in a perpetual treaty evolve (66) → apply: passengers and tourists covered (67–71).

cards.q: Can necessity terminate a treaty?
cards.a: No. Gabčíkovo: necessity under State responsibility only excuses non-performance while it lasts; termination requires a VCLT ground (Arts 54–64). Hungary's impossibility, fundamental change and material breach arguments all failed.

cards.q: Why do the ICJ and the IACtHR both interpret evolutively, but differently?
cards.a: The ICJ derives evolution from the parties' presumed common intention (generic terms in long treaties). The IACtHR derives it from the object and purpose of protecting individuals (living instrument, pro persona, Art 31(3)(c)). Pauwelyn and Elsig: institutional setting shapes method.

cards.q: Permissibility or opposability: what happens to a reservation incompatible with object and purpose?
cards.a: Permissibility school: it is invalid objectively, acceptance cannot cure it, and it may be severed so the State is bound without it (Belilos, Loizidou, Hilaire, HRC GC 24; ILC Guide 4.5.3 presumption). Opposability school: validity depends on the other parties' reactions. Practice is mixed: most objectors to the Maldives' CEDAW reservation kept treaty relations; Sweden treated consent as invalid.

cards.q: Has any court actually accepted a plea of fundamental change of circumstances?
cards.a: Only the ECJ in Racke (1998): the outbreak of civil war in Yugoslavia allowed the EC to suspend its trade agreement. The ICJ rejected it in Fisheries Jurisdiction (1973) and Gabčíkovo (1997, para 104); boundary treaties are excluded (Art 62(2)(a)), and a party cannot rely on a change it caused (Art 62(2)(b)).

excerpts.source: Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties (1969)
excerpts.text: Every treaty in force is binding upon the parties to it and must be performed by them in good faith.
excerpts.why: Pacta sunt servanda: the baseline that every termination or suspension argument (Arts 60–62) must overcome.

excerpts.source: Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties (1969)
excerpts.text: A treaty shall be interpreted in good faith in accordance with the ordinary meaning to be given to the terms of the treaty in their context and in the light of its object and purpose.
excerpts.why: One holistic rule (not a hierarchy); Art 32 travaux only to confirm or when the meaning is ambiguous or absurd.

topics.title: Custom, general principles and other sources
core: Art 38(1) ICJ Statute: treaties, custom, general principles; judicial decisions and teachings as subsidiary means. Beyond Art 38: unilateral declarations (Nuclear Tests 1974), binding SC decisions (Charter Arts 25, 103), soft law as evidence.
Two elements (North Sea para 77; ILC Conclusions 2018, Concl. 2–3): general practice and opinio juris, each assessed separately with regard to context.

Practice: primarily States, sometimes IOs (Concl. 4); physical and verbal acts, sometimes inaction (Concl. 6); widespread, representative and consistent (Concl. 8). Abstention counts only if based on a conscious duty (Lotus p 28). Asylum: 'uncertainty and contradiction … fluctuation and discrepancy' defeats custom. Nicaragua para 186: perfect consistency not required; breaches justified by exceptions confirm the rule.
Time: no fixed duration if practice is extensive and virtually uniform, including specially affected States (North Sea paras 73–74).

Opinio juris: a sense of legal obligation, not courtesy (North Sea para 77); can coexist with other motives. GA resolutions can evidence it depending on content, adoption and voting (Nuclear Weapons paras 70–73: only 'nascent' opinio juris against deterrence practice; Chagos paras 150–153: Res 1514 declaratory).

Induction versus deduction: Nicaragua (paras 184–188) effectively started from opinio juris in GA resolutions (Res 2625) and then checked practice; Kupreškić (ICTY 2000, paras 527–534) used the Martens Clause to let opinio necessitatis outweigh scarce practice (reprisals against civilians prohibited; tu quoque irrelevant) — criticised as deductive.

Treaty and custom: a treaty provision may codify, crystallise or generate custom (North Sea): generation needs a norm-creating provision, widespread and representative participation including specially affected States, extensive and virtually uniform practice, and opinio juris. Equidistance in Geneva Art 6 failed. Treaty and custom coexist with separate identities (Nicaragua paras 175–179; VCLT Art 43).

Climate AO 2025: the climate treaties are not a lex specialis excluding general IL; customary duties of due diligence and cooperation bind all States; a non-party must show equivalent conduct, otherwise it bears 'the full burden' (paras 309–315).

Regional and bilateral custom: the party relying on it must prove it binds the other (Asylum); bilateral custom exists (Right of Passage 1960; Costa Rica v Nicaragua para 141 on subsistence fishing). Persistent objector: consistent, open objection during formation (Fisheries 1951; ILC Concl. 15); never against jus cogens. A State that objects only after a rule has formed is normally bound, but Hernández recognises a 'subsequent objector': a State that accepted an existing rule and objects to its proposed modification is not bound by the changed rule if the others acquiesce (he reads Fisheries 1951 this way).

General principles (Art 38(1)(c)): principles of law generally (good faith, reparation — Chorzów), principles from domestic orders (res judicata, estoppel, burden of proof), principles of the international system (ex injuria jus non oritur). Ignore the anachronistic 'civilized nations'.

Subsidiary means (Art 38(1)(d)): no binding precedent (Art 59) but the ICJ follows its case law; the ILC, ILA, IDI, ICRC Customary IHL Study (contested by the US: Bellinger and Haynes). Equity infra, praeter, contra legem; ex aequo et bono only by consent (Art 38(2)).

Unilateral declarations (Nuclear Tests 1974): public, by a competent authority, with intent to be bound — binding without acceptance, read restrictively (ILC Guiding Principles 2006; DRC v Rwanda: the justice minister's statement was not specific enough). Hierarchy: no formal hierarchy among Art 38 sources, but jus cogens (VCLT 53, 64), Charter Art 103, erga omnes.

Sources architecture: formal sources (binding law-creation methods) versus material sources (evidence of a rule: judgments, ILC studies, resolutions, textbooks). Art 38 is technically the ICJ's lex arbitri but works as the authoritative statement of sources; the ILC's work is an 'indirect but influential' source. SC decisions bind under Art 25 and prevail under Art 103; Res 1373 (2001) laid down general rules close to 'legislating'. Soft law is non-binding (the term is 'misleading'): it can be a 'subterfuge' for inaction or point to future hard law (Stockholm and Rio; the ecocide proposal).

Relativity of custom (Hernández): acquiescence must be 'clear and consistent' (a high threshold). New States are bound by existing custom; a tabula rasa has been rejected even by new States. Bilateral custom exists (Right of Passage), but a State cannot claim a special custom exempting itself alone. Persistent objection examples: the US and Japan against expansive territorial-sea claims (1970s), China against restrictive immunity. Hernández warns that objector rules favour 'power asymmetries' and fragment general custom.

Jus cogens fine print: Art 53 requires 'double' recognition, as a norm of general international law and as non-derogable, by the international community of States as a whole (positivist; contrast the naturalists Orakhelashvili and Cassese, and Thirlway's custom-based view). ILC 2022 Conclusions: custom is the 'most common basis' (Concl. 5), there is no regional jus cogens, and all peremptory norms are erga omnes (Concl. 17). Candidates with some support: enforced disappearance, the right to life, non-refoulement. Effects: a treaty conflicting at conclusion is void ab initio in its entirety (Arts 53, 44(5)); one conflicting with a new peremptory norm terminates from then on (Arts 64, 71(2)); no derogation by reservation, custom or unilateral act; no circumstance precluding wrongfulness (Art 26). It confers neither jurisdiction (DRC v Rwanda) nor an exception to immunity (Germany v Italy). Abi-Saab: an 'empty box' waiting to be filled.
lecture: Lecture 5 (Marhold) restates the 'traditional framework' from Lotus ('International law governs relations between independent States …') before the two-element doctrine.

Practice questions on the slides: whose practice, what practice (ILC Conclusion 6: physical and verbal acts, inaction), abstention (Lotus), 'constant and uniform' (Asylum), time (North Sea), and how to read breaches (Nicaragua paras 186–188).

The working group adds the method debate: should custom be identified differently by field (immunities, continental shelf, environment, IHL)? Does judicial ethos matter — activism versus conservatism? One sentence of this earns originality marks.

cases.name: North Sea Continental Shelf (FRG v Denmark/Netherlands)
cases.holding: Equidistance in Geneva Art 6 was neither codified custom nor crystallised nor generated afterwards; custom needs settled practice and opinio juris (para 77); short time can suffice with extensive, virtually uniform practice including specially affected States.
cases.use: The two elements; treaty-to-custom routes.

cases.name: Asylum (Colombia v Peru)
cases.holding: Colombia failed to prove a regional custom of diplomatic asylum binding Peru: practice showed too much uncertainty and contradiction, and Peru had repudiated it.
cases.use: Regional custom; consistency; persistent objection.

cases.name: Fisheries (UK v Norway)
cases.holding: The ten-mile rule for bays was not general custom and in any event did not bind Norway, which had always opposed it.
cases.use: Persistent objector.

cases.name: Nuclear Tests (Australia/NZ v France)
cases.holding: France's public statements that it would stop atmospheric tests were binding unilateral undertakings, made with intent to be bound; the dispute had no object.
cases.use: Unilateral declarations.

cases.name: Prosecutor v Kupreškić
cases.holding: Reprisals against civilians are prohibited by custom; through the Martens Clause, principles of humanity and public conscience let opinio juris weigh more where practice is scarce; tu quoque has no place in IHL.
cases.use: Deductive custom-finding (and its critique).

cases.name: Obligations of States in respect of Climate Change (AO)
cases.holding: The climate treaties do not exclude general IL; customary duties of due diligence to prevent significant harm and to cooperate bind all States; non-parties bear the full burden of showing equivalent conduct.
cases.use: Treaty–custom interaction; due diligence.

cards.q: What are the three treaty-to-custom routes (North Sea)?
cards.a: A treaty provision may (1) codify existing custom, (2) crystallise an emerging rule at the time of adoption, or (3) generate a new rule through later practice — which needs a norm-creating provision, widespread and representative participation including specially affected States, extensive and virtually uniform practice, and opinio juris.

cards.q: Why did the ICJ turn to custom in Nicaragua, and what did it say about treaty and custom?
cards.a: The US multilateral treaty reservation barred applying the Charter. The Court held custom exists and applies independently even with identical content to a treaty (paras 175–179); a jurisdictional bar on the treaty does not remove the parallel customary rule.

cards.q: How is Nicaragua's custom method criticised compared with North Sea?
cards.a: North Sea demanded extensive practice and was sceptical of inferring opinio juris from treaty participation; Nicaragua deduced opinio juris from consent to GA resolutions (Res 2625) and then treated inconsistent practice as breaches. Explained by the subject matter (force), but inconsistent.

cards.q: Conditions for the persistent objector rule?
cards.a: Objection expressed clearly, made known to other States, and maintained consistently while the rule is forming (Fisheries; ILC Concl. 15). Not available against jus cogens; objecting after the rule has formed normally comes too late (but see Hernández on the 'subsequent objector' resisting a modification); new States are bound by existing custom.

cards.q: When is a unilateral declaration binding?
cards.a: When made publicly by an authority competent to bind the State, with intent to be bound (Nuclear Tests); no acceptance or quid pro quo needed; interpreted restrictively (ILC Guiding Principles 2006; DRC v Rwanda).

cards.q: Three types of general principles?
cards.a: Principles of law generally (good faith, full reparation — Chorzów); principles drawn from domestic legal orders (res judicata, estoppel, burden of proof); principles formed within the international system (ex injuria jus non oritur, proportionality).

cards.q: Treaty in conflict with jus cogens: what is the difference between Art 53 and Art 64 VCLT?
cards.a: Art 53: conflict at conclusion, so the whole treaty is void ab initio (no severance, Art 44(5)) and the parties must eliminate the consequences of acts performed under it (Art 71(1)). Art 64: a new peremptory norm emerges, so the treaty becomes void and terminates from then on, and rights acquired earlier survive so far as their maintenance does not conflict with the new norm (Art 71(2)).

excerpts.source: North Sea Continental Shelf (Germany v Denmark; Germany v Netherlands)
excerpts.text: Not only must the acts concerned amount to a settled practice, but they must also be such, or be carried out in such a way, as to be evidence of a belief that this practice is rendered obligatory by the existence of a rule of law requiring it.
excerpts.why: The two elements, practice and opinio juris; equidistance had not crystallised into custom.

excerpts.source: Military and Paramilitary Activities in and against Nicaragua (Nicaragua v US)
excerpts.text: …instances of State conduct inconsistent with a given rule should generally have been treated as breaches of that rule, not as indications of the recognition of a new rule. If a State acts in a way prima facie incompatible with a recognized rule, but defends its conduct by appealing to exceptions or justifications contained within the rule itself… the significance of that attitude is to confirm rather than to weaken the rule.
excerpts.why: Why widespread violations of Art 2(4) do not destroy the customary prohibition.
