topics.title: Jus ad bellum
core: Art 2(4) UN Charter prohibits the threat or use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of any State. It is also customary law (Nicaragua) and widely regarded as jus cogens.
Only two Charter exceptions: (1) Security Council authorisation under Chapter VII (Art 39 determination, then Art 42 measures), and (2) individual or collective self-defence under Art 51.

Self-defence needs an armed attack, meaning the 'most grave forms' of the use of force (Nicaragua para 191 for 'most grave forms'; para 195 for 'scale and effects' and for frontier incidents and arms supply). Frontier incidents and arms supply are not armed attacks.

Custom adds necessity and proportionality (Nicaragua para 176; Nuclear Weapons para 41). Measures must be reported to the SC (Art 51) and are allowed only until the SC has taken the necessary measures. Failing to report does not by itself make self-defence unlawful; in custom it is evidence that the State did not believe it was acting in self-defence (Nicaragua para 200; DRC v Uganda para 145).
Collective self-defence requires the victim State to declare itself attacked and to request help (Nicaragua paras 195–199).

The State claiming self-defence bears the burden of proving the armed attack, and that it was the target. An attack must be 'specifically aimed' at it, and accumulation of events can count (Oil Platforms paras 51, 57–64).

Non-state actors: an armed attack by armed bands counts where they are 'sent by or on behalf of' a State, or the State has 'substantial involvement' (Res 3314 Art 3(g); Nicaragua para 195). The Wall AO (para 139) read Art 51 as covering armed attack 'by one State against another State' and rejected Israel's claim because the attacks were not imputable to a foreign State and the threat came from territory Israel controls. DRC v Uganda (paras 146–147) found the ADF attacks not attributable to the DRC, and expressly left open 'whether and under what conditions' international law allows self-defence against large-scale attacks by irregular forces. State practice since 9/11 and the 'unwilling or unable' doctrine remain contested.

Anticipatory self-defence against an imminent attack is debated (Caroline formula: 'instant, overwhelming, leaving no choice of means'). Pre-emptive self-defence against non-imminent threats is not lawful.

Intervention by invitation: valid consent from the government in effective control precludes wrongfulness (Art 20 ARSIWA; DRC v Uganda paras 42–53). Consent must be real, and its withdrawal ends the justification.
Humanitarian intervention or R2P without SC authorisation has no clear legal basis. Corfu Channel rejected a 'right of intervention' as a manifestation of a policy of force.

Lesser uses of force short of an armed attack violate Art 2(4) and the non-intervention principle (coercion in matters within domestic jurisdiction, Nicaragua para 205). Third States have no right of 'collective' armed response to acts that are not an armed attack (Nicaragua para 211), and only the victim State could take 'proportionate counter-measures' (para 249). The Court expressly left open what direct reactions, possibly involving force, the victim itself may take (para 210). Today ARSIWA Art 50(1)(a) bars countermeasures involving force.

Proportionality in self-defence is measured against what is needed to halt and repel the attack (and recover territory), not against the size of the initial attack: a lawful response 'may well have to assume dimensions disproportionate to those of the attack suffered'. ICJ practice looks at the scale of the whole operation, its geographic reach into the target State (DRC v Uganda para 147: airports and towns hundreds of kilometres from the border) and the weapons used. Necessity means no non-forcible means of repelling the attack; in Oil Platforms it failed because the US had never complained about the platforms' military use and called one strike a 'target of opportunity'.

'Against the territorial integrity or political independence' is not a loophole for 'limited' force. Corfu Channel rejected the UK's minesweeping as 'the manifestation of a policy of force'; Nicaragua rejected a restrictive reading; and the Eritrea–Ethiopia Claims Commission held that force used to recover territory a State claims is unlawfully occupied still breaches Art 2(4), since otherwise border disputes would make 'a large and dangerous hole' in the rule. Compare the claims over Goa (1961), the Falklands (1982), Kuwait (1990) and China's position on Taiwan.

Self-defence against non-State actors, three positions. (1) Restrictive, the ICJ's case law on its face: the armed attack must be attributable to a State (Res 3314 Art 3(g)). (2) Middle: Judges Higgins and Buergenthal (Wall) and Kooijmans and Simma (DRC v Uganda) say Art 51 does not require a State attacker, but force in the host State must be confined to the group and strictly necessary and proportionate. (3) Expansive, 'unwilling or unable': the US, UK, Australia, Canada and Turkey in Syria from 2014. Hernández: the 'most plausible' argument is that an unwilling or unable host is effectively 'aiding and abetting', but most scholars are sceptical because the acting State decides alone that the test is met. One innovative view (Paddeu) treats self-defence against non-State actors as a circumstance precluding wrongfulness rather than an Art 51 exception.

Hernández on Gaza (2023–): the 7 October attacks meet the factual threshold of an armed attack, but Art 51 fits poorly. Self-defence cannot be directed against Palestine (its statehood is contested by Israel itself) or rest on attribution to it, and Gaza remains occupied territory (SC Res 2720 (2023), preamble; OPT AO 2024 para 93: Israel kept 'key elements of authority'). So the Wall AO para 139 logic applies: Israel's powers there come from the law of occupation. Hezbollah in Lebanon (from Sept 2024) is a cross-border case for the non-State actor debate, and necessity and proportionality apply in any event.

Anticipatory versus pre-emptive self-defence in UN and expert texts: the 2004 High-level Panel and the 2005 'In Larger Freedom' report say imminent threats 'are fully covered by Article 51', while non-imminent threats go to the SC; IDI Resolution 10A (2007) accepts only an 'actual or manifestly imminent' armed attack. Practice: the SC unanimously condemned Israel's 1981 strike on Iraq's Osirak reactor as a 'clear violation of the Charter' (Res 487); Israel did not plead anticipatory self-defence in 1967; the 2002 Bush Doctrine, dropping imminence, went 'considerably beyond the bounds of international law'. DRC v Uganda para 148: Art 51 does not allow force 'to protect perceived security interests'.

Protection of nationals abroad has been claimed as self-defence by the US (Dominican Republic 1965, Grenada 1983, Panama 1989, the failed 1980 Tehran rescue), Israel (Entebbe 1976), the UK (Suez 1956), France, and Russia (Georgia 2008, Crimea 2014). The SC has rarely condemned it, largely because of the veto, but its legality 'remains contentious'. In an answer, argue it at most as a narrow form of self-defence and check necessity and proportionality strictly.

Collective security details: the SC's Art 39 discretion is wide. It has found a 'breach of the peace' only four times (Korea 1950, Falklands 1982, Iran–Iraq 1987, Kuwait 1990) and has never formally determined an 'act of aggression'. The SC must act within the Purposes and Principles (Art 24(2)) and, arguably, jus cogens, but Art 103 lets its decisions prevail over other treaty obligations. Korea (Res 83, 1950), adopted while the USSR was absent, became the blueprint for authorising Member States. The GA has used Uniting for Peace (Res 377 (V)) eleven times when the veto blocks the SC (e.g. ES-11/1 on Ukraine). Regional enforcement action needs SC authorisation (Art 53).

Humanitarian intervention in practice: most interventions that looked humanitarian were justified as self-defence (India in Bangladesh 1971, Tanzania in Uganda 1979, Vietnam in Cambodia 1979). Only the UK (Iraq no-fly zones; Kosovo) and Belgium (before the ICJ in 1999) pleaded humanitarian intervention as law. Res 1244 neither endorsed nor condemned NATO, and the G77 rejected the doctrine (1999). Hernández: the negative reactions to Kosovo 'seem to confirm the unlawfulness' of unilateral humanitarian intervention and led to R2P, whose third pillar runs through SC authorisation. The call on the P5 not to use the veto is only 'a polite intimation'.

Hernández's closing argument (useful for 'Is Art 2(4) dead?'): law 'functions simultaneously to constrain and to facilitate violence', so one should not presume 'a linear progression towards stronger rules against using force'. 'The arc of history does not bend unequivocally towards peace.'
lecture: History arc the lecture uses: just war theory (12th–17th c.) → League Covenant Art 12 (procedural limits only) → Kellogg-Briand Pact 1928 (renounced war, Germany, Japan, Italy were parties) → Art 2(4).

Art 2(4) elements flagged on the slides: 'international relations' (international character), the threat of force (Nuclear Weapons AO), and the open question whether economic coercion counts (the dominant view: no, it falls under non-intervention).
Status: customary (Nicaragua) and jus cogens, with the consequence that a treaty conflicting with it is void (VCLT Arts 53, 64).
Exceptions listed as three: self-defence, Chapter VII, and consent.
Art 51 requirements on the slides: armed attack, reporting to the SC (not a customary condition, cf. Nicaragua), necessity, proportionality. 'Inherent' signals a pre-existing customary right.
Collective self-defence: the victim State must itself meet the conditions and must request help.

Anticipatory versus pre-emptive self-defence, illustrated with Israel's Defence Minister in Feb 2026 calling strikes on Iran a 'pre-emptive attack … to remove threats' — a claim that, on its own terms, falls outside Art 51.
Chapter VII ladder: Art 39 (threat to the peace), Art 40 (provisional measures), Art 41 (non-forcible measures), Art 42 (force). Authorisation formula: 'all necessary means' (Res 678 (1990), Kuwait).

Contested extensions: non-state actors after 9/11 and 'unwilling or unable'; humanitarian intervention (Kosovo 1999, no SC authorisation); R2P operating through SC authorisation (Libya 2011, Res 1973).

'Is Art 2(4) dead?' — examples: Iran 2025/26, Ukraine 2014/2022, Gaza 2023, Venezuela 2026 (US forces at Maduro's compound), Greenland 2026, Cambodia/Thailand 2025. Three responses: (1) it was always like this (Franck, 'Who killed Article 2(4)?': national self-interest wins), yet Hathaway and Shapiro (The Internationalists) argue the ban did reduce conquest; (2) this time is different, because States no longer bother with legal justifications (contrast the UK Attorney General's 2003 Iraq 'revival' argument based on Res 678, 687, 1441); (3) does it matter? Systemic consequences, compliance, legitimacy, reputation, and multilateralism.

'Is Art 2(4) dead?' — examples: Iran 2025/26, Ukraine 2014/2022, Gaza 2023, Venezuela 2026 (US forces at Maduro's compound), Greenland 2026, Cambodia/Thailand 2025. Dated facts: Israel–Iran 12-day war 13–24 June 2025, with US strikes 22 June under collective self-defence (Art 51 letter 27 June 2025). US–Israel war on Iran from 28 Feb 2026 (Khamenei killed; US Art 51 letter 10 Mar 2026; ceasefire 8 Apr 2026). US capture of Maduro 3 Jan 2026, framed as 'law enforcement' plus Art 51 and condemned at the SC on 5 Jan. Greenland threats Jan 2026 (threat of force, tariffs). Cambodia–Thailand 24–28 July and Dec 2025 (dueling Art 51 letters). India–Pakistan 7–10 May 2025.

cases.name: Corfu Channel (UK v Albania)
cases.holding: Albania was responsible for not warning of mines it knew about: every State must not knowingly allow its territory to be used for acts contrary to the rights of others. The UK's minesweeping 'Operation Retail' violated Albanian sovereignty, and there is no 'right of intervention'.
cases.use: Due diligence over territory; rejecting self-help or intervention arguments.

cases.name: Nicaragua v US (Merits)
cases.holding: Art 2(4) and self-defence also exist in custom. An armed attack is the gravest form of force; arming and training the contras was a use of force and intervention but not an armed attack. Collective self-defence needs a declaration and a request. There is no collective countermeasure against a non-armed-attack intervention.
cases.use: Gravity threshold; armed bands; requirements of collective self-defence; non-intervention.

cases.name: Legality of Nuclear Weapons AO
cases.holding: Self-defence is subject to necessity and proportionality whatever weapon is used. A threat of force is unlawful if the force threatened would be unlawful.
cases.use: Necessity and proportionality; the threat of force.

cases.name: Wall AO
cases.holding: Art 51 recognises self-defence in case of armed attack by one State against another. Israel could not rely on Art 51 against attacks from territory it controlled (occupied territory) and not imputable to a foreign State (para 139).
cases.use: Self-defence against non-state actors (restrictive view); occupied territory.

cases.name: Oil Platforms (Iran v US)
cases.holding: The US failed to prove that Iran was responsible for the attacks on the Sea Isle City and the Samuel B. Roberts, or that they were aimed at the US. The attacks on the platforms were not shown to be necessary (para 76). On proportionality, the 1988 strikes, part of the wider Operation Praying Mantis, were not proportionate; the 1987 strike might have been proportionate had it been necessary (para 77).
cases.use: Burden of proof; 'specifically aimed'; accumulation of events; necessity of the targets.

cases.name: Armed Activities (DRC v Uganda)
cases.holding: Uganda's presence was lawful while the DRC consented, and unlawful after consent was withdrawn. The ADF attacks were not attributable to the DRC, so the conditions for self-defence were not met. Uganda's actions were a grave violation of Art 2(4), and Uganda was an occupying power in Ituri.
cases.use: Consent and its withdrawal; non-state actors; the Art 51 reporting requirement.

cases.name: Russian letter to the UN, 24 Feb 2022 (S/2022/154)
cases.holding: Russia invoked Art 51 (individual and collective self-defence of the 'DPR' and 'LPR' and of Russia against NATO threats) and the protection of people from 'genocide'. GA Res ES-11/1 deplored this as aggression.
cases.use: Sample abusive self-defence claim: no armed attack, no recognised State to request collective self-defence, no imminence.

cases.name: Kosovo intervention (NATO)
cases.holding: NATO bombed the FRY without SC authorisation, invoking a humanitarian catastrophe. The Independent International Commission called it 'illegal but legitimate'. No general right of humanitarian intervention emerged.
cases.use: Humanitarian intervention argument and its weakness.

cases.name: Libya (SC Res 1973)
cases.holding: The SC authorised 'all necessary measures' to protect civilians, the first R2P-based authorisation. Critics argue the coalition went beyond civilian protection to regime change.
cases.use: R2P works through Chapter VII, not around it.

cases.name: Iraq 2003 (UK Attorney General's advice)
cases.holding: The UK argued authority to use force revived from the combined effect of Res 678, 687 and 1441. Most scholars reject the 'revival' theory.
cases.use: How States justify force; the 'this time is different' response in the lecture.

cases.name: US Art 51 letter on 'Operation Epic Fury' (Iran)
cases.holding: Letter of 10 Mar 2026: strikes on Iran from 28 Feb 2026 are 'necessary and proportionate actions in exercise of the inherent right of self-defense', also 'in the collective self-defense of Israel', citing Iran's long-running attacks via proxies. No specific imminent armed attack identified.
cases.use: Testing imminence (Caroline) and accumulation of events (Oil Platforms) against a pre-emptive rationale; collective self-defence requires the victim's request (Nicaragua para 199).

cases.name: US Art 51 letter on strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities
cases.holding: Letter of 27 June 2025 (S/2025/426): strikes of 22 June on Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan were collective self-defence of Israel, 'necessary and proportionate', directed solely at the nuclear programme. Iran replied (S/2025/436) that Art 51 requires an armed attack that 'occurs'.
cases.use: Anticipatory vs pre-emptive self-defence; the role of Art 51 reporting.

cases.name: US capture of Maduro (Venezuela)
cases.holding: US forces seized Maduro in Caracas on 3 Jan 2026. The US called it a 'law enforcement operation' supported by the military (Noriega analogy) and invoked Art 51. Most SC members, including US allies, criticised it as a violation of the Charter.
cases.use: Art 2(4) and political independence; no armed attack, consent or SC authorisation; also head-of-State immunity ratione personae (Arrest Warrant) and male captus.

cases.name: SC Res 2803 (Gaza: Board of Peace and International Stabilization Force)
cases.holding: Adopted 17 Nov 2025 (13–0–2). Endorses the US peace plan, welcomes a Board of Peace as transitional administration and authorises an International Stabilization Force to use 'all necessary measures' until 31 Dec 2027.
cases.use: Chapter VII authorisation formula ('all necessary measures'), the SC's continued relevance, and self-determination concerns.

cases.name: Eritrea–Ethiopia Claims Commission, Jus ad Bellum (Ethiopia's Claims 1–8)
cases.holding: Eritrea's May 1998 resort to armed force around Badme breached Art 2(4) and was not self-defence. A State may not use force to recover territory it claims is unlawfully occupied: such an exception would create 'a large and dangerous hole in a fundamental rule of international law'.
cases.use: No 'territorial claim' exception to Art 2(4); answers the argument that force restoring one's own territory is not 'against territorial integrity'.

cases.name: Israeli strike on Osirak (SC Res 487)
cases.holding: The SC unanimously condemned Israel's strike on an Iraqi nuclear reactor under construction as a 'clear violation of the Charter'. Israel had claimed a right of pre-emption against future nuclear weapons; the US read the condemnation as limited to the facts.
cases.use: Preventive or pre-emptive self-defence rejected by the SC; contrast with the 2025–26 strikes on Iran in the notes.

cards.q: What are the only two Charter exceptions to Art 2(4)?
cards.a: SC authorisation under Chapter VII (Arts 39 and 42) and self-defence under Art 51. Consent is not an exception: where it is valid there is no use of force against the State at all (or Art 20 ARSIWA).

cards.q: What threshold does Nicaragua set for an armed attack?
cards.a: The 'most grave forms' of the use of force, judged by scale and effects. Sending armed bands of sufficient gravity counts. Supplying weapons or logistical support does not.

cards.q: What are the conditions for collective self-defence?
cards.a: An armed attack on the victim State, its declaration that it has been attacked, its request for help, necessity and proportionality, and a report to the SC.

cards.q: Who carries the burden of proof in self-defence, and what did Oil Platforms add?
cards.a: The State invoking self-defence must prove it was the victim of an armed attack attributable to the other State and specifically aimed at it. The targets struck must also be necessary (a military objective linked to the attack).

cards.q: What does Res 3314 Art 3(g) cover?
cards.a: Sending by or on behalf of a State armed bands, groups, irregulars or mercenaries that carry out acts of armed force of such gravity as to amount to listed acts, or substantial involvement therein. It is the customary benchmark for indirect armed attack (Nicaragua para 195).

cards.q: What is the Caroline formula?
cards.a: The necessity of self-defence must be 'instant, overwhelming, leaving no choice of means, and no moment for deliberation'. It is the basis of the anticipatory self-defence debate.

cards.q: Can a State respond with force to an intervention that is not an armed attack?
cards.a: Not lawfully: self-defence needs an armed attack, and countermeasures may not involve force (ARSIWA Art 50(1)(a)). Nicaragua held that only the victim may take proportionate countermeasures and that third States have no right of collective armed response (paras 211, 249), but it expressly left open whether the victim's own reaction may involve force (para 210).

cards.q: What are Franck's thesis and the counter-view in 'Is Art 2(4) dead?'
cards.a: Franck (1970): the Charter's normative system failed because national self-interest, especially of the superpowers, overrides treaty obligations. Counter-view: Hathaway and Shapiro show the outlawry of war sharply reduced territorial conquest. The lecture adds that what changed recently is that States increasingly stop offering legal justifications at all.

cards.q: Is economic coercion a 'use of force' under Art 2(4)?
cards.a: The prevailing view is no: 'force' means armed force (travaux; Res 2625). Economic coercion is addressed by the non-intervention principle (Nicaragua para 205; Res 2625; OAS resolutions).

cards.q: Pre-emptive versus anticipatory self-defence, with the lecture's example.
cards.a: Anticipatory: against an imminent attack (Caroline), debated. Pre-emptive: against a non-imminent future threat, unlawful. Example: Israel's Defence Minister (Feb 2026) described strikes on Iran as a 'pre-emptive attack … to remove threats', which fails the imminence requirement.

cards.q: How did States justify the 2025 Cambodia–Thailand and India–Pakistan uses of force?
cards.a: Cambodia–Thailand (24–28 July 2025; Dec 2025): both sides claimed Art 51 and accused the other of aggression (Thailand at the SC 25 July 2025; dueling letters 9–10 Dec 2025); ceasefire 28 July and KL Joint Declaration 26 Oct 2025. India–Pakistan (7–10 May 2025): India's Operation Sindoor answered the Pahalgam attack as a 'right to respond' to cross-border terrorism, without a formal Art 51 letter; Pakistan invoked Art 51. Shows frontier incidents vs armed attack (Nicaragua para 191) and non-State attribution (para 195).

cards.q: Was the Greenland episode (Jan 2026) a breach of Art 2(4)?
cards.a: Possibly a prohibited threat of force: a threat is unlawful if the threatened force would itself be unlawful (Nuclear Weapons AO para 47), and acquisition of territory by force is prohibited (Res 2625). US statements refusing to rule out force, then ruled out at Davos, plus tariff threats (economic coercion falls under non-intervention, not Art 2(4)). Denmark told the SC it was a prohibited threat.

cards.q: Is proportionality in self-defence measured against the size of the armed attack?
cards.a: No. It is measured against what is needed to halt and repel the attack and recover territory, so it may exceed the original attack. The ICJ weighs the scale of the whole operation, its reach into the target State (DRC v Uganda para 147) and the weapons used. Necessity asks whether there was any non-forcible way to repel the attack (Oil Platforms: no prior complaint, 'target of opportunity').

cards.q: Nicaragua para 195 versus para 115: what does each test do?
cards.a: Para 195 (with Res 3314 Art 3(g)) decides when an attack by armed bands counts as an armed attack by a State for Art 51: sending them, or substantial involvement, with sufficient scale and effects. Para 115 (effective control) decides whether a group's conduct is attributable to a State for State responsibility (ARSIWA Art 8). Do not mix them: one is jus ad bellum, the other attribution.

cards.q: How can a State be responsible for a proxy group without the group's acts being attributable to it?
cards.a: DRC v Uganda paras 160–165: the MLC was not a Ugandan organ and acted on no instructions or control, so its acts were not attributable. But Uganda's own training and military support breached non-intervention and Art 2(4) (Res 2625; Nicaragua paras 206, 209), whatever its motive (para 163). Three layers: (1) own troops' force; (2) no attribution of the group's acts; (3) responsibility for its own support. Nicaragua has the same structure.

cards.q: What are the two readings of the Wall AO para 139?
cards.a: Broad: Art 51 covers only armed attacks by one State against another, so attacks not attributable to a State never trigger it (the Court's wording). Narrow: the decisive point was that the attacks came from territory Israel itself occupies, where its powers come from the law of occupation; on this reading the AO says nothing about attacks from a foreign State's territory and can be reconciled with Res 1368/1373. Hernández's Gaza analysis relies on the occupation point.

cards.q: Has the SC ever determined an 'act of aggression' under Art 39?
cards.a: No. It has found a 'breach of the peace' four times (Korea 1950, Falklands 1982, Iran–Iraq 1987, Kuwait 1990); most determinations are of a 'threat to the peace', read widely (intra-State violence, terrorism, even Ebola). The 2022 condemnation of Russia's 'aggression' came from the GA (ES-11/1) under Uniting for Peace.

topics.title: Jurisdiction and immunities
core: There are three types of jurisdiction: prescriptive (making law), adjudicative (courts) and enforcement (arrest, seizure). Enforcement is strictly territorial without consent (Lotus, p. 18).

Bases of prescriptive jurisdiction: territoriality, either subjective (the act starts here) or objective (it is completed or takes effect here, the effects doctrine); active nationality (the offender is a national); passive personality (the victim is a national, accepted for terrorism and serious crimes); protective principle (vital State interests such as currency or security); universal jurisdiction (piracy, grave breaches, torture, genocide, CAH, war crimes).

Lotus presumption: States may extend their laws unless a prohibitive rule exists. Today this is heavily criticised: in Arrest Warrant, President Guillaume and the Joint Separate Opinion (Higgins, Kooijmans, Buergenthal) treated the Lotus dictum as belonging to a laissez-faire era since overtaken, and most modern scholarship requires a permissive basis. Judge Van den Wyngaert, by contrast, relied on Lotus (no prohibitive rule) to support universal jurisdiction in absentia.
Universal jurisdiction in absentia is contested. In Arrest Warrant the Joint Separate Opinion (Higgins, Kooijmans, Buergenthal) accepted it with safeguards, while President Guillaume rejected it.

State immunity is restrictive: acta jure imperii (sovereign acts) are immune, acta jure gestionis (commercial acts) are not (UN Convention 2004, Arts 5, 10–17). It is a procedural bar, separate from the lawfulness of the conduct (Germany v Italy para 93).

Immunity ratione personae belongs to the troika (Head of State, Head of Government, Foreign Minister) and diplomats. It covers all acts, official and private, but only while in office, and it is absolute before foreign national courts, even for international crimes (Arrest Warrant paras 51–61).

Immunity ratione materiae covers official acts of all State officials and continues after office. It is debated whether it covers international crimes: Pinochet said no for torture under CAT. ILC draft Art 7 (first reading 2022) listed genocide, CAH, war crimes, apartheid, torture and enforced disappearance; on second reading (completed May 2026, now draft art 6 [7]) aggression, slavery and the slave trade were added. The list remains controversial (recorded votes; codification versus progressive development).

Arrest Warrant para 60: immunity does not mean impunity. Para 61 lists four avenues: prosecution in their own State; waiver by their own State; after leaving office, by another State's court with jurisdiction, for acts committed before or after the period of office and for acts committed during office in a private capacity; and certain international criminal courts with jurisdiction.

Before international courts, Art 27 Rome Statute removes official capacity. Art 98 creates tension with cooperation duties (Al-Bashir Jordan Appeal 2019: no customary head-of-State immunity before international courts).
Jus cogens and immunity: there is no conflict, because the rules operate on different planes, procedural versus substantive (Germany v Italy paras 92–97; Al-Adsani).

Immunity before international and hybrid courts, 2025–26: ICC PTC II (Tajikistan, referred 7 May 2026) and PTC I (Hungary, 24 July 2025) applied Art 27 against non-party Heads of State (Putin, Netanyahu). The Ukraine Special Tribunal (CoE treaty) instead respects the troika's personal immunity while in office (Art 23(5)) but removes functional immunity (Art 23(4)). This is evidence that States still treat immunity ratione personae as unresolved outside the ICC.

Russian Central Bank assets (about €185–210bn, mostly at Euroclear, Belgium): the EU immobilised them indefinitely (Council decision, 12 Dec 2025) instead of six-monthly unanimous renewal. The 'reparations loan' failed (Belgian opposition: immunity from execution, UNCSI Art 21(1)(c) central-bank property, litigation risk). The European Council (18–19 Dec 2025) chose a €90bn EU-borrowed loan for 2026–27, reserving the right to use the assets. Exam frame: an immobilisation is not confiscation; using the principal needs a countermeasures justification (ARSIWA Arts 49–53: reversibility, injured-State or Art 54 'non-injured State' debate) plus an answer to enforcement immunity.

Hernández on Lotus: the passage is 'invariably quoted' for a permissive presumption, 'yet this is not fully accurate'. Objecting States never accept that they must prove a prohibitive rule; they reply that the acting State has 'no right'. A linking point is required, and only territoriality and nationality are firmly established, so a State legislating beyond its territory and nationals bears the burden of justifying it. Any basis must at least be 'tolerated by other States'. Use this to argue burden of proof in a jurisdiction question.

Effects doctrine: US v Alcoa (1945) took jurisdiction over a foreign cartel's intended effects on the US market; the Helms–Burton Act (1996) met EU and UK 'blocking statutes'. The CJEU in Intel v Commission (2017, para 49) adopted a 'qualified effects test': EU competition law applies where it is foreseeable that conduct will have an 'immediate and substantial effect' in the EU. Contrast Ben El Mahi v Denmark (ECtHR 2006): effects abroad of the Danish cartoons created no jurisdictional link under the ECHR.

Passive personality remains unsettled as custom but is accepted by treaty: Hostages Convention Art 5(1)(d) (Hernández cites it as Art 9), Tokyo Convention Art 4(b), Terrorism Financing Convention Art 7(2)(a). Hernández stresses its imperial pedigree (nineteenth-century unequal treaties and capitulations; the Cutting case of 1886, where the US protested Mexico's claim) and why it is resented: it implies the territorial State's legal system is deficient. The protective principle is limited to essential State functions (security, currency, immigration documents), not, for example, sexual offences abroad or antitrust.

Universality: piracy jurisdiction rests on a pragmatic rationale (the high seas are beyond any State's jurisdiction: 'common interest and mutual convenience'), not on heinousness, so keep it apart from universal jurisdiction over international crimes. Most States now require a minimal link: Belgium amended its law in 2003 after US and Israeli pressure (the Sharon complaint; the threat to NATO headquarters funding). Argentina is the outlier with 'pure' universal jurisdiction (Rohingya complaint 2019; warrant for Maduro, Sept 2024). Aut dedere aut judicare is treaty-based, not custom (Belgium v Senegal applied only CAT Art 7), and there is no duty to open universal civil jurisdiction for torture (Naït-Liman v Switzerland, ECtHR GC 2018).

Immunity is a procedural bar, distinct from 'act of State' (a substantive rule that courts will not adjudicate a foreign State's sovereign acts in its own territory) and non-justiciability. Belhaj v Straw (UKSC 2017) treats non-justiciability as a narrow sub-category of act of State; Kuwait Airways (HL 2002) refused to apply the doctrine to Iraq's seizure of aircraft because the invasion of Kuwait was a flagrant breach of international law. In a problem, deal with immunity first, then act of State.

Who is the 'State' for immunity: UNCSI Art 2(1)(b) covers organs; federal units and State agencies only if they are entitled to perform AND actually perform sovereign acts (cumulative; the UK SIA is similar, the US FSIA broader). Separate State entities are presumed distinct, and 'quite extreme circumstances' are needed to treat them as the State (Gécamines, Privy Council). A central bank's commercial letter of credit is not immune (Trendtex, 1977). Waiver may be express or implied: prior written agreement, bringing proceedings, or taking steps in them.

Restrictive immunity in practice: about two-thirds of States apply it and one-third still apply absolute immunity (2015 study); Russia (2016) and China (2024) switched to restrictive. UNCSI is still not in force (22 of the 30 ratifications needed). Exceptions to note: employment contracts, but not for staff doing governmental functions (Benkharbouche, UKSC 2017: embassy domestic workers can sue); territorial tort (Art 12), limited to physical injury or damage caused on forum territory, e.g. Al Masarir v Saudi Arabia (EWHC 2022) on spyware hacking devices in the UK. On nature versus purpose, UNCSI Art 2(2) lets purpose count only if agreed or under forum practice; I Congreso del Partido (HL 1981) looks at the 'whole context', but governmental motive cannot turn a commercial act into a sovereign one.

Hernández's critique of Germany v Italy: the Court chose to lay down a general rule, and its strict procedural/substantive split ignores developments in other courts and elevates judge-made procedural canons over substantive norms. It could have decided on narrower grounds: Germany had paid reparations and Italy had waived further claims in the 1961 agreements. His broader point: there is no 'linear progress from sovereignty to human rights' in the law of immunities.

Officials, three refinements. (1) Territorial exception: functional immunity does not cover crimes committed by a foreign official on the forum State's territory where that State consented neither to the official's presence nor to the activity (assassination, sabotage, espionage); Khurts Bat (EWHC 2011): a Mongolian intelligence chief's alleged abduction in Germany. (2) Immunity belongs to the State and can be waived by it (the Philippines for Marcos; Chad for Habré). (3) Head-of-State immunity is breached only by a 'constraining act of authority': a French judge's invitation to Djibouti's President to testify did not violate it (Djibouti v France, 2008).

Diplomatic and consular law (VCDR and VCCR codify custom; a 'self-contained regime', per Tehran Hostages). Mission premises are inviolable and the receiving State must protect them (VCDR Art 22; the 2024 Ecuadorian raid on Mexico's embassy, now before the ICJ). Agrément can be refused and a diplomat declared persona non grata 'at any time' without reasons (Art 9). Diplomatic agents have full criminal immunity and civil immunity subject to Art 31(1): private immovable property, succession, and private professional or commercial activity (Wong v Basfar, UKSC 2022: exploiting a domestic worker in modern-slavery conditions fell within 'commercial activity'). Consuls have only functional immunity and can be arrested for a 'grave crime' (VCCR Arts 41, 43). A receiving State may object to a designation of mission premises only if its objection is timely, non-arbitrary and non-discriminatory (Equatorial Guinea v France, 2020).
lecture: Starting point: domaine réservé — nationality is for each State to confer, but international law decides its limits and consequences (Nottebohm).

Territoriality quoted from Island of Palmas (1928): sovereignty means independence, the exclusive right to exercise State functions over a portion of the globe. Domestic examples: Dutch Criminal Code s.2; Swiss Criminal Code Art 8 (place of act and place of effect).

Nationality: active personality (Dutch CC s.5(2), double criminality), passive personality (Dutch CC s.5b for listed serious offences against Dutch nationals). Ships and aircraft have the nationality of registration (Chicago Convention Arts 17–18).

Corporate nationality: renvoi to domestic law (incorporation or seat); no genuine-link requirement (Barcelona Traction). Why it matters: treaty shopping, as in Philip Morris v Australia (restructuring to gain BIT protection, claim dismissed as abuse of rights).
Universal jurisdiction is primarily treaty-based: CAT Art 6(1) (custody of a present offender) and Art 7(1) (extradite or prosecute). Rationale: heinousness gives all States an interest (cf. piracy).

State immunity sources: custom built from domestic court practice; UN Convention on Jurisdictional Immunities 2004 (not in force, parts reflect custom); European Convention on State Immunity 1972; VCDR and VCCR. Immunity is a procedural bar decided before the merits.

Sovereign versus commercial acts: what counts is the nature of the act, not its purpose (US v Irsa, Italian Court of Cassation 1963: a public works contract is private in nature even if it serves a public end).

Enforcement immunity of State property is stricter. Mixed-use embassy bank accounts are immune (Philippine Embassy, German Constitutional Court 1977, followed in the UK, NL, Belgium; codified in UNCSI Art 21). Central-bank property is protected only where clearly linked to monetary policy; a sovereign wealth fund was not immune (Ascom v Kazakhstan, Swedish Supreme Court 2021). Topical: on 2 Sept 2026 Norway attached the Russian vessel Professor Molchanov at Svalbard to enforce Naftogaz's 2023 Crimea investment award against Russia, and a Norwegian court upheld the attachment (reported Oct 2026). Russia claims it is a State scientific vessel (UNCSI Arts 19, 21).

Officials: ratione personae attaches to office, is needed for the function, belongs to the troika, and covers acts 'during or prior to' office (ILC draft Art 4(2), 2022). Ratione materiae attaches to official acts. The ILC's crimes exception (first-reading Art 7, revised by the Drafting Committee in 2025, renumbered draft art 6 [7]) excludes functional immunity for genocide, CAH, war crimes, aggression, apartheid, torture, enforced disappearance, slavery and slave trade. Adopted on second reading 15 May 2026 after a 23–4–3 recorded vote.

cases.name: SS Lotus (France v Turkey)
cases.holding: Turkey could prosecute the French officer because the effects of the collision were felt on the Turkish ship (objective territoriality). Restrictions on independence are not presumed. Enforcement outside territory is prohibited.
cases.use: Permissive presumption (to criticise); enforcement is territorial; effects.

cases.name: Nottebohm (Liechtenstein v Guatemala)
cases.holding: Nationality conferred without a 'genuine connection' could not be opposed to Guatemala for diplomatic protection.
cases.use: Nationality as a basis of jurisdiction and protection; genuine link.

cases.name: Arrest Warrant (DRC v Belgium)
cases.holding: Issuing and circulating an arrest warrant against the incumbent DRC Foreign Minister violated his full immunity and inviolability. There is no customary exception for war crimes or CAH. The Court did not decide on universal jurisdiction.
cases.use: The troika's immunity ratione personae; para 61 avenues; the universal jurisdiction debate (separate opinions).

cases.name: Van den Wyngaert dissent, Arrest Warrant
cases.holding: The Court should have considered international criminal law and the fight against impunity. Universal jurisdiction in absentia is permitted under Lotus and there is no prohibitive rule. She would have found no immunity for core crimes.
cases.use: The counter-argument for accountability.

cases.name: R v Bow Street, ex parte Pinochet (No 3)
cases.holding: Lord Browne-Wilkinson: torture, under the CAT definition, cannot be an official function attracting immunity ratione materiae once the UK, Spain and Chile were all CAT parties. A former Head of State can be extradited.
cases.use: Functional immunity does not cover torture (former officials only).

cases.name: Al-Adsani v UK
cases.holding: Granting Kuwait immunity in a civil torture claim did not violate the Art 6 right of access to court. Immunity pursues a legitimate aim and is proportionate. No accepted jus cogens exception exists for civil suits.
cases.use: Civil State immunity versus jus cogens; dissent on the hierarchy of norms.

cases.name: Jurisdictional Immunities (Germany v Italy)
cases.holding: Italy violated Germany's immunity by allowing civil claims for Nazi-era crimes. Acts of armed forces in armed conflict are acta jure imperii. The territorial tort exception does not cover them. Neither the gravity of the violation, jus cogens, nor 'last resort' removes immunity.
cases.use: The procedural nature of immunity; the leading case against the jus cogens exception.

cases.name: Philippine Embassy case
cases.holding: A general current account used for an embassy's expenses serves diplomatic functions and is immune from execution, even if individual payments are commercial.
cases.use: Mixed-use accounts; immunity from execution (UNCSI Art 21).

cases.name: Ascom v Kazakhstan
cases.holding: Central-bank protection covers only property clearly connected with monetary policy. A sovereign wealth fund built from oil revenues for unspecified future needs was not immune from execution.
cases.use: Limits of central-bank and State-property immunity.

cases.name: US v Irsa
cases.holding: A public works contract is private (jure gestionis) in nature even though it serves a public purpose: the nature of the act decides, not its purpose.
cases.use: Nature versus purpose test.

cases.name: Barcelona Traction (Belgium v Spain)
cases.holding: A company's national State (incorporation and seat) protects it, not the shareholders' State. No genuine-link requirement for corporations. Famous obiter on erga omnes obligations (para 33).
cases.use: Corporate nationality; erga omnes (links to Week 11).

cases.name: ILC Draft Articles on Immunity of State Officials from Foreign Criminal Jurisdiction (second reading)
cases.holding: 17 draft articles adopted 15 May 2026. Draft art 6 [7]: immunity ratione materiae shall not apply to genocide, CAH, war crimes, aggression, apartheid, torture, enforced disappearance, slavery and slave trade; procedural safeguards in Arts 8–17 (notification, consultation, transfer). Convention recommended 20 July 2026.
cases.use: Current state of the 'international crimes exception' debate (Pinochet vs Germany v Italy, Arrest Warrant).

cases.name: Attorney-General of Israel v Eichmann
cases.court: District Court of Jerusalem (affirmed by the Supreme Court of Israel, 1962)
cases.holding: Israel could try Eichmann for crimes against the Jewish people and war crimes: besides universality (delicta juris gentium), the court relied on the protective principle, with the 'crime against the Jewish people' as the linking point. His abduction from Argentina violated Argentina's sovereignty, not his rights, and the breach was 'cured' by Argentina's waiver in a joint communiqué.
cases.use: Shows that a judgment usually rests on several jurisdictional bases; illegal enforcement abroad (abduction) does not by itself bar trial (male captus, bene detentus), but it is a wrong against the territorial State.

cases.name: Intel v European Commission (C-413/14 P)
cases.holding: EU competition law may be applied to a US company's rebates to manufacturers outside the EU under a 'qualified effects test': it is justified under public international law when it is foreseeable that the conduct will have an immediate and substantial effect in the EU.
cases.use: The modern, limited version of the effects doctrine (objective territoriality).

cases.name: Khurts Bat v Investigating Judge of the German Federal Court
cases.court: High Court of England and Wales
cases.holding: The head of Mongolia's intelligence agency could be extradited to Germany for an alleged abduction committed there on Mongolia's instructions: he had no special-mission immunity, and functional immunity does not cover acts done on another State's territory without its consent to the presence or the activity.
cases.use: The territorial exception to immunity ratione materiae; covert operations abroad.

cards.q: What are the five bases of prescriptive jurisdiction?
cards.a: Territoriality (subjective, objective, effects), active nationality, passive personality, the protective principle, and universality.

cards.q: Immunity ratione personae versus ratione materiae: who, what, and when?
cards.a: Personae: the troika and diplomats, all acts, only while in office, absolute before foreign courts. Materiae: any official, official acts only, continues after office.

cards.q: What are the four Arrest Warrant para 61 avenues?
cards.a: Prosecution in their own State; waiver by their State; after office, for acts before or after office or private acts during it; before an international criminal court with jurisdiction.

cards.q: Why doesn't jus cogens override State immunity in Germany v Italy?
cards.a: The rules address different matters. Immunity is procedural and decides whether a court may exercise jurisdiction, not whether the conduct was lawful, so there is no conflict.

cards.q: What did Pinochet decide, and what are its limits?
cards.a: A former Head of State has no functional immunity for torture under the CAT regime, because torture can't be an official function. It concerns criminal proceedings against a former official, not incumbents, and not civil suits against States.

cards.q: What is the Lotus principle, and why is it criticised?
cards.a: Whatever is not prohibited is permitted, so States may extend jurisdiction absent a prohibitive rule. Critics say it is outdated and inconsistent with sovereign equality; modern practice requires a recognised permissive basis.

cards.q: Why is enforcement immunity stricter than adjudicative immunity?
cards.a: Execution against State property interferes more directly with sovereignty. Even if a court can hear a claim (commercial exception), property is only attachable if in commercial use and not covered by specific protections (diplomatic accounts, central-bank property, military property): UNCSI Arts 19–21; Philippine Embassy; Ascom.

cards.q: What did the ILC adopt on officials' immunity?
cards.a: Draft Art 4(2) (2022, kept): ratione personae covers all acts of the troika, private or official, during or prior to office. The second reading was completed in May 2026 with 17 draft articles (A/CN.4/L.1034). Former Art 7 is now Art 6 [7]: no ratione materiae immunity before foreign criminal courts for genocide, CAH, war crimes, aggression, apartheid, torture, enforced disappearance, slavery and the slave trade (aggression, slavery and the slave trade were added in 2025). Adopted after a recorded vote and contested as lex ferenda (thin State practice). Part Four sets procedural safeguards (notification, invocation and waiver, transfer of proceedings).

cards.q: Assad sample question: which jurisdictional bases does Germany have?
cards.a: Universal jurisdiction for war crimes, CAH and torture (CAT Arts 5(2) and 7 since he is present; VStGB). Passive personality for the 10 German victims. Not territoriality (acts in Syria), not active nationality, and the protective principle fails: refugee costs are not a vital State interest threatened by the offence.

cards.q: May the EU confiscate immobilised Russian central-bank assets to fund Ukraine?
cards.a: Freezing is a reversible measure. Confiscation breaches State immunity from execution (central-bank property, UNCSI Art 21(1)(c), Art 19) unless justified as a countermeasure (ARSIWA Arts 49–53: reversibility, proportionality; for non-directly-injured States the Art 54 'lawful measures' debate). The EU (Dec 2025) kept the assets frozen indefinitely and chose a €90bn borrowed loan instead of the 'reparations loan'.

cards.q: Why is universal jurisdiction over piracy different from universal jurisdiction over torture?
cards.a: Piracy: a pragmatic rule, because pirates operate on the high seas outside any State's jurisdiction (UNCLOS Arts 101, 105). Torture, genocide and similar crimes: jurisdiction justified by their gravity, mostly through treaties (CAT Arts 5(2), 7: custody plus extradite or prosecute). Most States now require a link such as the offender's presence (Belgium after 2003); aut dedere aut judicare is a treaty duty, not custom.

cards.q: Immunity, act of State and non-justiciability: what is the difference?
cards.a: Immunity is a procedural bar tied to the defendant (the State or its official) and decided first (Germany v Italy para 93). Act of State is a substantive rule that a court will not rule on the validity of a foreign State's sovereign acts in its own territory. Non-justiciability bars certain sensitive political questions (Belhaj, UKSC 2017: a narrow sub-category). Kuwait Airways (HL 2002): public-policy exception for flagrant breaches of international law.

cards.q: When can a foreign intelligence officer not rely on functional immunity?
cards.a: When the territorial exception applies: the crime was committed on the forum State's territory and that State consented neither to the official's presence nor to the activity (Khurts Bat, EWHC 2011). The ILC's draft articles leave this exception out of the crimes list because territorial sovereignty already covers it. Also check special-mission immunity (needs the receiving State's consent to the mission).

cards.q: Can the receiving State arrest a diplomat or a consul suspected of a crime?
cards.a: A diplomatic agent: no. They are inviolable (VCDR Art 29) and immune from criminal jurisdiction (Art 31); remedies are waiver by the sending State (Art 32) or declaring them persona non grata (Art 9). A consular officer: only for a 'grave crime' and by a judicial decision (VCCR Art 41(1)); they have immunity only for official acts (Art 43).

excerpts.source: SS Lotus (France v Turkey)
excerpts.text: Far from laying down a general prohibition to the effect that States may not extend the application of their laws and the jurisdiction of their courts to persons, property and acts outside their territory, it leaves them in this respect a wide measure of discretion…
excerpts.why: The permissive Lotus principle for prescriptive jurisdiction; contrast the strict territoriality of enforcement jurisdiction.

excerpts.source: Arrest Warrant of 11 April 2000 (DRC v Belgium)
excerpts.text: It has been unable to deduce from this practice that there exists under customary international law any form of exception to the rule according immunity from criminal jurisdiction and inviolability to incumbent Ministers for Foreign Affairs, where they are suspected of having committed war crimes or crimes against humanity.
excerpts.why: Personal immunity of the troika is absolute while in office, even for international crimes.

excerpts.source: Arrest Warrant (DRC v Belgium)
excerpts.text: Accordingly, the immunities enjoyed under international law by an incumbent or former Minister for Foreign Affairs do not represent a bar to criminal prosecution in certain circumstances.
excerpts.why: The four routes: trial at home; waiver; after office, for acts before or after office or private acts; certain international criminal courts.

topics.title: International economic law
core: Core GATT disciplines: Art I most-favoured-nation treatment, Art III national treatment for 'like products', Art XI elimination of quantitative restrictions, Art II tariff bindings.

Art XX general exceptions use a two-tier test: (1) provisional justification under a paragraph, such as (b) measures necessary to protect human, animal or plant life or health, or (g) measures relating to the conservation of exhaustible natural resources made effective with domestic restrictions; (2) the chapeau: no arbitrary or unjustifiable discrimination where the same conditions prevail, and no disguised restriction on trade (US–Shrimp).

Art XXI security exceptions: a measure the member 'considers necessary' for essential security interests, taken in time of war or another emergency in international relations. Russia–Traffic in Transit held it is not fully self-judging. The panel checks objectively that there is an emergency, and the member must articulate its interests in good faith with a minimum plausibility link.

Process and production methods: Tuna-Dolphin I (unadopted) refused import bans based on how tuna was caught and on extraterritorial goals. US–Shrimp softened this with a sufficient nexus (migratory turtles) and evolutionary interpretation.

Investment law: BITs and the Energy Charter Treaty provide fair and equitable treatment, protection against expropriation without compensation (ECT Art 13), full protection and security, and investor–State arbitration. Withdrawals took effect for the UK (2025) and the EU/Euratom (28 June 2025) after several EU States left, subject to the 20-year sunset clause (Art 47(3)). The modernised ECT applies provisionally from 3 Sept 2025.

NIEO Declaration (GA Res 3201 (S-VI), 1974): permanent sovereignty over natural resources, including the right to nationalise, and the Global South's critique of the economic order. The formula that compensation disputes are settled under the nationalising State's domestic law comes from the Charter of Economic Rights and Duties of States (GA Res 3281 (XXIX), 1974, Art 2(2)(c)).

Factory at Chorzów (Merits, 1928) is the reparation standard: reparation must, as far as possible, wipe out all the consequences of the illegal act. German Interests in Polish Upper Silesia (1926) held that expropriation contrary to the Geneva Convention is unlawful, and that municipal law is a fact before the international court.
Links to State responsibility: necessity defences in investment cases (CMS, LG&E) and security exceptions function as treaty-specific circumstances precluding wrongfulness.

Current WTO crisis (2025–26): Appellate Body vacant since Dec 2019. The US blocked the 130-member appointment proposal for the 99th time on 24 July 2026 and again on 27 Oct 2026, so panel reports can be appealed 'into the void' (MPIA as workaround). MC14 (Yaoundé, 26–30 Mar 2026) produced no reform declaration, and the e-commerce moratorium lapsed. US tariffs: China's complaints DS633 (Feb 2025) and DS638 ('reciprocal' tariffs, Apr 2025), with the US claiming Art XXI makes them non-justiciable. The US Supreme Court held IEEPA does not authorise tariffs (Learning Resources v Trump, 20 Feb 2026); s.122 tariffs replaced them.

Compensation for expropriation, two standards. Capital-exporting States: the Hull formula, 'prompt, adequate and effective' (Hull's note to Mexico, 1938; ECT Art 13). Capital-importing States: 'appropriate compensation' (GA Res 1803 (1962)), settled under the nationalising State's law (CERDS Art 2(2)(c), 1974). Texaco v Libya (1977) treated Res 1803, which Western States had supported, as custom but gave the CERDS clause no opinio juris. Texaco and Aminoil (1982) read 'appropriate' close to Hull, and the 1992 World Bank Guidelines define 'appropriate' as 'adequate, effective and prompt' (constructive ambiguity).

Lawful versus unlawful expropriation. A lawful taking must serve a public purpose (read broadly, including police powers, social and economic reform and the environment), be non-discriminatory, not arbitrary or vindictive, follow due process, and be compensated. Compensation is then the investment's value at the moment of dispossession, without future profits (Amoco v Iran, IUSCT 1987). An unlawful taking triggers Chorzów full reparation, including lost profits and possibly a later valuation date (Yukos: valued at the date of the award). Indirect expropriation: interference that makes rights 'so useless that they must be deemed to have been expropriated', even if title remains (Starrett Housing v Iran, IUSCT 1983).

BIT protection beyond FET: 'investment' is broadly defined (a contribution, a certain duration, risk, and a contribution to the host State's development), indirect investments through local subsidiaries are covered, and the investment must have been made in accordance with host-State law. FET is tied to the international minimum standard, and full protection and security is a robust duty that applies even in armed conflict. National treatment and MFN apply (MFN can import better standards from other BITs; ECT Art 16). ISDS bypasses local remedies, unlike diplomatic protection, and once the host State consents to ICSID the investor's home State may not exercise diplomatic protection (ICSID Art 27). There is no appeal, only annulment (Art 52). Denunciations: Bolivia 2007, Ecuador 2009 (rejoined 2021), Venezuela 2012, Honduras 2024.

WTO enforcement is a special countermeasures regime. If the losing Member does not comply within the reasonable period, the DSB may authorise the winner to suspend concessions ('retaliation', DSU Art 22): first in the same sector, then other sectors or agreements (Art 22(3)), at a level equivalent to the nullification or impairment (arbitration under Art 22(6)–(7)). EC–Hormones is the leading example. Because DSU Art 23 bars unilateral determinations, general-law countermeasures for WTO breaches are excluded: a lex specialis under ARSIWA Art 55.

Art XXI and the ICJ: in Nicaragua (1986, para 222) the ICJ held that the US–Nicaragua FCN Treaty's security clause was not self-judging precisely because, unlike GATT Art XXI, it lacked the words 'which it considers'. Russia–Traffic in Transit later read those words as making only 'necessary' self-judging. Follow-ups: in Saudi Arabia–IPRs (2020) one measure (not acting against the pirate broadcaster beoutQ) failed the plausibility test; in Dec 2022 panels found US steel and aluminium tariffs and the 'made in China' marking rule for Hong Kong goods were not 'taken in time of' an emergency (the US appealed into the void).

Yukos and treaty law: Russia signed but never ratified the ECT. The tribunal read Art 45(1)'s proviso ('to the extent ... not inconsistent with its constitution, laws or regulations') as asking whether provisional application as such was consistent with Russian law, so the arbitration clause applied (cf VCLT Art 25). The taxation carve-out (Art 21) covers only bona fide taxation. The Hague District Court set the awards aside (2016); the Court of Appeal reinstated them (2020); the Dutch Supreme Court dismissed Russia's final appeal on 17 Oct 2025. Russia–Transit and Yukos both 'look behind the label' (security, taxation).

Hernández's framing: international economic law is 'not a neutral framework' but an outgrowth of colonial economic relations. The NIEO was not radical (it used the language of sovereignty and consent) and ended as a 'relative failure'. The neoliberal Bretton Woods consensus has 'survived almost wholly intact', its institutions are dominated by powerful States, and IMF/World Bank loan conditionality imposes structural adjustment; the AIIB and the BRICS New Development Bank are alternatives. Developing States gained only GATT Part IV (1965, non-reciprocity) and the 1979 Enabling Clause (optional 'differential and more favourable treatment').
lecture: IEL under pressure: backlash against globalisation, trade wars since 2016, supply-chain vulnerability and 'economic security' (energy, raw materials, semiconductors), an emerging multipolar order, a paralysed WTO (Appellate Body crisis since 2019), and contested investor–State arbitration.

Origins: Bretton Woods 1944 (World Bank, IMF), GATT 1947, BITs from 1959, the NIEO 1974 (participation in lawmaking, permanent sovereignty over natural resources, regulating TNCs, fair commodity prices, technology transfer), WTO 1995 (166 members).

Rationales: Ricardo's comparative advantage ('size of the pie'), terms-of-trade theory (reciprocal binding avoids an inefficient Nash equilibrium; Bagwell and Staiger), credibility towards domestic lobbies, and preventing trade wars (Smoot-Hawley 1930). Distribution matters: the Lakner–Milanovic 'elephant graph'.

WTO dispute settlement is compulsory (Art 6.1 DSU, negative consensus), exclusive (Art 23.1 DSU: no unilateral determinations, no other court decides WTO breaches) and contentious (no advisory opinions).
Like products (Philippines – Distilled Spirits): physical characteristics, end use, tariff classification, consumer tastes and preferences. Non-product-related PPMs are the hard case.

Art XX two-tier test (US – Gasoline, US – Shrimp): first a paragraph, then the chapeau, cumulatively. Under (b) the Member chooses its level of protection (Brazil – Retreaded Tyres) but must use the least trade-restrictive reasonably available measure (Thailand – Cigarettes); once necessity is shown, the complainant must prove an alternative (US – Gambling). Under (g) 'exhaustible natural resources' is read widely (clean air in US – Gasoline; living turtles in US – Shrimp) and 'relating to' needs only a rational connection, so environmental cases go under (g).

Art XXI has no chapeau. It lay dormant 1947–2016: Sweden's 1975 footwear restrictions on 'security' grounds (withdrawn), and the 1985 US embargo on Nicaragua, where the panel was barred from judging the invocation.

Investment law: protection against direct or indirect expropriation without compensation, a public-purpose requirement (German Interests in Polish Upper Silesia: 'public utility, judicial liquidation and similar measures'), national and MFN treatment. Origins in protecting Global North assets after decolonisation (Suez 1956).

cases.name: US — Restrictions on Imports of Tuna (Tuna-Dolphin I)
cases.holding: A US import ban on tuna caught with dolphin-unsafe methods violated Art XI and could not be justified under Art XX(b) or (g), which do not protect resources outside the importing State's jurisdiction. Measures cannot regulate production methods abroad.
cases.use: The traditional view against extraterritorial and production-method measures.

cases.name: US — Shrimp (AB)
cases.holding: Sea turtles are 'exhaustible natural resources' (evolutionary interpretation using UNCLOS and CITES). The measure related to conservation under Art XX(g), but failed the chapeau because it was applied rigidly, without negotiation, in an arbitrary and unjustifiably discriminatory way.
cases.use: The two-tier Art XX test; environmental measures; the chapeau.

cases.name: Russia — Traffic in Transit
cases.holding: Panels have jurisdiction over Art XXI. The existence of an 'emergency in international relations' (here Russia–Ukraine 2014) is objectively determinable. Members define their own essential security interests in good faith, but measures must meet a minimum plausibility requirement. Russia's measures were justified.
cases.use: Security exceptions are justiciable; the scope of self-judging clauses.

cases.name: Yukos Universal v Russia
cases.holding: Russia's tax measures against Yukos amounted to an indirect expropriation under ECT Art 13. Across the three parallel Yukos shareholder awards (Hulley, Yukos Universal, Veteran), damages assessed at about USD 66.7bn were reduced by 25% for contributory fault, to about USD 50bn in total (Yukos Universal's own share was about USD 1.8bn).
cases.use: Investment protection; expropriation; contributory fault (Art 39 ARSIWA analogy).

cases.name: German Interests in Polish Upper Silesia / Chorzów Factory
cases.holding: Poland's expropriation of German-owned property breached the Geneva Convention. The 1928 merits judgment set the full-reparation standard: restitution in kind or its monetary equivalent, so as to wipe out the consequences.
cases.use: Unlawful expropriation; the reparation standard (Art 31 ARSIWA).

cases.name: US — Gasoline
cases.holding: Established the two-tier analysis of Art XX. Clean air as an exhaustible natural resource was the panel's finding, which was not appealed. The measure was justified under (g) but failed the chapeau.
cases.use: Order of analysis; wide reading of (g).

cases.name: Brazil — Retreaded Tyres
cases.holding: Members may set their own level of health and environmental protection; necessity is a weighing exercise and an import ban can be necessary if it contributes materially to the aim.
cases.use: Art XX(b) necessity.

cases.name: Philippines — Distilled Spirits
cases.holding: Likeness under Art III judged by physical characteristics, end use, tariff classification and consumer preferences, with competition between the products at the core.
cases.use: National treatment, 'like products'.

cases.name: Texaco Overseas Petroleum v Libya
cases.holding: Libya's nationalisation of oil concessions breached the concession contracts. GA Res 1803 (1962), adopted with broad support including capital-exporting States, reflected custom on permanent sovereignty and 'appropriate compensation'; the compensation clause of the Charter of Economic Rights and Duties of States (Art 2(2)(c)) lacked opinio juris because the main capital-exporting States opposed it.
cases.use: GA resolutions as evidence of custom (links to week 5); the compensation debate (Hull v 'appropriate').

cases.name: Amoco International Finance Corp v Iran
cases.holding: Distinguished lawful from unlawful expropriation: for a lawful taking, compensation is the value of the undertaking at the date of dispossession, without future lost profits; only an unlawful taking calls for full Chorzów reparation including lucrum cessans.
cases.use: Quantum depends on whether the taking was lawful (public purpose, non-discrimination, due process, compensation).

cases.name: EC — Measures Concerning Meat and Meat Products (Hormones)
cases.holding: The EC's ban on hormone-treated beef breached the SPS Agreement because it was not based on a proper risk assessment (Art 5) or international standards (Art 3). When the EC failed to comply, the US and Canada were authorised in 1999 to suspend concessions equivalent to their losses (DSU Art 22.7); the dispute ended in a mutually agreed solution.
cases.use: WTO retaliation as an institutionalised countermeasure; science-based limits on health measures.

cards.q: What is the two-tier test under GATT Art XX?
cards.a: (1) The measure falls within a paragraph, e.g. (b) is 'necessary' to protect health (weighing and balancing, less trade-restrictive alternatives), or (g) 'relates to' conservation and is even-handed. (2) It meets the chapeau: no arbitrary or unjustifiable discrimination and no disguised restriction.

cards.q: Is GATT Art XXI self-judging after Russia–Traffic in Transit?
cards.a: Partly. 'Which it considers' applies to necessity and to defining security interests (subject to good faith and plausibility). Whether there is war or an emergency in international relations is objective and reviewable by the panel.

cards.q: Why does US–Shrimp matter beyond trade law?
cards.a: It uses systemic and evolutionary interpretation (VCLT Art 31(3)(c)), integrating environmental treaties into WTO law and accepting measures with a nexus to a resource beyond the regulating State's territory.

cards.q: What is the Chorzów Factory formula?
cards.a: Reparation must, as far as possible, wipe out all the consequences of the illegal act and re-establish the situation that would in all probability have existed had the act not been committed.

cards.q: Why is WTO dispute settlement called compulsory, exclusive and contentious?
cards.a: Compulsory: a panel is established unless the DSB decides by consensus not to (Art 6.1 DSU). Exclusive: Members must use the DSU to redress WTO breaches and may not decide unilaterally (Art 23.1 DSU). Contentious: no advisory opinions, only rulings in disputes.

cards.q: Why invoke Art XX(g) instead of (b)?
cards.a: (g) only requires the measure to 'relate to' conservation (a rational connection) and to be even-handed with domestic restrictions, which is more deferential than (b)'s 'necessary' (least trade-restrictive alternative). Exhaustible resources are read widely, so environmental measures usually go under (g).

cards.q: EU raw-materials mock: China's claims and the EU's defences?
cards.a: Claims: lower tariffs for 'friendly nations' breach MFN (Art I:1) and bindings (Art II); quotas on Chinese imports breach Art XI (and possibly XIII). Defences: Art XXI(b)(iii) emergency in international relations (objectively reviewable after Russia – Traffic in Transit; plausibility and good faith), Art XX(j) short supply or (g) only with difficulty; any regional-integration exception (Art XXIV) does not cover a political 'friends' list.

cards.q: Can the US rely on Art XXI GATT to shield its 2025 tariffs from WTO review?
cards.a: The US says Art XXI is self-judging and non-justiciable (DS633, DS638). Russia–Traffic in Transit (2019) holds that panels review whether an 'emergency in international relations' objectively exists and whether measures meet a minimum plausibility and good-faith test. Generalised 'reciprocal' tariffs on all trading partners are hard to tie to an emergency. Even a winning complainant faces an appeal into the void because the AB is non-functional (99th US block, July 2026).

cards.q: How does compensation differ for lawful and unlawful expropriation?
cards.a: Lawful (public purpose, non-discriminatory, due process, compensation offered): the value of the investment at the time of the taking, usually without future profits (Amoco v Iran). Unlawful: full reparation under Chorzów, which can include lost profits and a later valuation date (Yukos valued at the award date). The standard itself is disputed: Hull ('prompt, adequate and effective') versus 'appropriate' (Res 1803; Texaco).

cards.q: What does Nicaragua (1986) para 222 add to the debate on GATT Art XXI?
cards.a: The ICJ held the US–Nicaragua treaty's security clause was not self-judging because it lacked the words 'which it considers', which GATT Art XXI contains. So the wording matters: Russia–Transit treats 'which it considers' as making only necessity self-judging, while the existence of an emergency stays objective. Compare the ICJ's good-faith review of a self-judging clause in Djibouti v France (2008, para 145).

cards.q: How is WTO retaliation different from a countermeasure under general international law?
cards.a: It needs a prior panel/AB ruling and DSB authorisation after non-compliance; it follows a sector sequence (DSU Art 22(3)); its level must be equivalent to the nullification or impairment, checked by arbitration; and unilateral countermeasures for WTO breaches are barred (DSU Art 23). General countermeasures (ARSIWA Arts 49–53) are self-judged and need only a prior wrong, a demand and proportionality.
