topics.title: State responsibility I: the wrongful act
core: Art 1 ARSIWA: every internationally wrongful act of a State entails its responsibility. Art 2: an internationally wrongful act is conduct (act or omission) that is (a) attributable to the State and (b) a breach of an international obligation. Damage and fault are not general requirements.

Art 4: conduct of any State organ, of any branch or level, is attributable. De facto organs count where there is 'complete dependence' on the State (Bosnia Genocide paras 392–393; Nicaragua para 110).
Art 5: persons or entities empowered by law to exercise governmental authority, acting in that capacity. Art 6: organs placed at the disposal of the State by another State.
Art 7: ultra vires acts of organs are still attributable if the organ acted in its official capacity.

Art 8: private persons acting on the instructions of, or under the direction or control of, the State. The ICJ's test is effective control over the specific operation (Nicaragua para 115; Bosnia Genocide paras 400–407). The ICTY in Tadić (Appeals, paras 115–145) used overall control for organised groups, but the ICJ rejected it for State responsibility (Bosnia para 404), confining it to conflict classification.

Art 9: conduct in the absence of official authorities. Art 10: insurrectional movements that become the new government. Art 11: conduct acknowledged and adopted by the State as its own (Tehran Hostages para 74: the approval given by Iran's authorities and their decision to perpetuate the occupation turned the militants' continuing occupation into acts of Iran; mere approval or endorsement is not adoption, per the ILC Commentary to Art 11).

Arts 12–15 (breach): breach is determined by the obligation's terms; the obligation must be in force at the time (Art 13); continuing wrongful acts extend over the whole period (Art 14); composite acts (Art 15).

Art 16 (aid or assistance), Art 17 (direction and control) and Art 18 (coercion) give derived responsibility in connection with another State's act. Aid requires knowledge, and the act must also be wrongful if committed by the assisting State.

Due diligence is a separate route: if conduct isn't attributable, ask whether the State breached its own obligation to prevent, an obligation of conduct measured by its capacity to influence (Bosnia Genocide paras 430–431; Corfu Channel).

Circumstances precluding wrongfulness (Arts 20–25): consent, self-defence, countermeasures, force majeure, distress, necessity. None justifies a breach of jus cogens (Art 26). Under Art 27, the duty to comply resumes once the circumstance ends, and compensation for material loss remains possible.
Force majeure (Art 23): irresistible force or unforeseen event beyond control making performance materially impossible, not merely more difficult. It is unavailable if the State contributed to it.
Distress (Art 24): the author had no other reasonable way to save their own life or the lives of persons in their care.

Necessity (Art 25), very strict and cumulative: the only way to safeguard an essential interest against a grave and imminent peril; it does not seriously impair an essential interest of the other State or the international community; the obligation doesn't exclude necessity; and the State has not contributed to the situation (Gabčíkovo paras 51–58).

Tehran Hostages shows the two routes to responsibility for private conduct. Phase one, the attack (paras 56–68): the militants were not organs and had not been 'charged by some competent organ ... to carry out a specific operation' (para 58); Khomeini's general anti-American statements were not an authorisation (para 59). So the attack was not attributable, but Iran was responsible for its own omission: it knew of the danger, had the means, and 'failed altogether to take any appropriate steps' to protect the mission (VCDR Art 22(2); paras 61–68). Phase two, the occupation (para 74): approval 'and the decision to perpetuate' the occupation made the militants agents of the State (ARSIWA Art 11). Approval alone is not adoption.

Art 7 (ultra vires) in the cases: Caire (France v Mexico, 1929) and Youmans (US v Mexico, 1926): officers or soldiers who use the powers or means of their office engage the State even when they disobey orders. Mallén (1927): an off-duty private assault was not attributable, but a later assault by the same official using his authority was. Modern examples: Velásquez Rodríguez (IACtHR 1988) and the Khashoggi killing (UN Special Rapporteur, 2019). The test is apparent authority (acting 'under colour' of office), not compliance with instructions.

Timing of breach: Art 13, the obligation must bind the State when the act occurs (Le Louis, 1817: the slave trade before the prohibition crystallised). Art 14: an expropriation is complete when it happens even if its effects continue, but a continuing denial of access to property is a continuing breach (Loizidou v Turkey, ECtHR). Gabčíkovo para 79: preparatory acts (works that 'could have been abandoned') are not yet a breach; para 80: a duty to mitigate affects the amount of compensation but cannot justify a wrongful act. Rainbow Warrior: the breach continued until the obligation expired on 22 July 1989; responsibility for earlier breaches remained, but there was nothing left to cease.

Status of the ARSIWA: GA Res 56/83 (12 Dec 2001) only 'takes note' of them, and a convention has been repeatedly deferred. Courts treat key articles as custom (Gabčíkovo para 52 on necessity; Bosnia Genocide on Arts 4, 8 and 16). Caron's 'paradox of form and authority': because the text looks like a treaty, tribunals may apply it like a statute. Ask article by article whether it codifies custom or develops the law; Arts 41(1), 48(2)(b) and 54 were openly presented as progressive development.

Climate Change AO (23 July 2025) on responsibility: breaches of climate obligations are internationally wrongful acts under the general law of State responsibility. A State's failure to take appropriate action to protect the climate system, including through fossil-fuel production, consumption, exploration licences or subsidies, may be an internationally wrongful act attributable to it. Reparation requires a 'sufficiently direct and certain causal nexus'.
lecture: ARSIWA history: early codification efforts, ILC first reading 1949–1996, second reading 1998–2001, the 2001 Articles 'noted' by the GA (not a treaty, largely custom).
Structure taught: Part 1 (attribution, breach, CPW), Part 2 (content: reparation, peremptory norms), Part 3 (implementation: invocation, countermeasures).

Attribution articles on the slides: Art 4 (organs, including police and courts), Art 5, Art 7 (ultra vires), Art 8 (effective control: Nicaragua and Bosnian Genocide; financing and training are not enough; cf. Tadić), Art 10 (insurrection becoming government), Art 11 (acknowledgment). Illustrated with the CIA 'Argo' operation story.
Breach (Art 12): conduct 'not in conformity with what is required of it by that obligation'; note the question of preparatory acts.
CPWs are a 'shield rather than a sword', may be justifications or excuses, and leave the underlying obligation intact.

Argentina cases: the 2001 crisis hit utilities paid in US dollars and indexed to US inflation. BIT Art XI ('measures necessary for the maintenance of public order … essential security interests') versus customary necessity: the CMS annulment committee faulted the tribunal for not considering Art XI on its own terms. ICSID enforcement: consent (Art 25), recognition 'as if it were a final judgment' (Art 54(1)), but no waiver of immunity from execution (Art 55).
Arts 26–27: no CPW for jus cogens; compliance resumes once the CPW ends, without prejudice to compensation (CMS, LG&E, Gabčíkovo).

cases.name: Gabčíkovo-Nagymaros (Hungary/Slovakia)
cases.holding: Hungary's ecological necessity argument failed: the peril was not 'imminent', other means were available, and Hungary contributed. Necessity does not terminate a treaty; it only excuses non-performance while it lasts. Slovakia's Variant C was a disproportionate countermeasure.
cases.use: The leading necessity analysis; countermeasure proportionality; necessity versus treaty termination.

cases.name: Rainbow Warrior (New Zealand/France)
cases.holding: France invoked distress and force majeure for removing agents Mafart and Prieur from Hao. The evacuation of Mafart for urgent medical care was justified by distress, but France breached its obligation by not returning him once the danger passed. Prieur's removal (pregnancy, a dying father) was not justified. The declaration of wrongfulness was itself satisfaction.
cases.use: Distress versus force majeure; the temporal limit of excuses (Art 27); satisfaction.

cases.name: CMS Gas v Argentina
cases.holding: Argentina's 2001–02 crisis measures were not justified by customary necessity: the measures weren't the only way and Argentina contributed. The tribunal read the BIT's Art XI emergency clause through Art 25. The annulment committee (2007) found the tribunal had erred by conflating Art XI with customary necessity, but held this was not an annullable error; it annulled only the umbrella-clause finding, so the damages award stood.
cases.use: Strictness of necessity; relation between a treaty clause and custom.

cases.name: LG&E v Argentina
cases.holding: On a similar crisis, the tribunal accepted that Argentina was in a state of necessity from December 2001 to April 2003, exempting it from compensation for that period under BIT Art XI.
cases.use: Shows divergent outcomes; temporal scope of necessity.

cases.name: Nicaragua v US (attribution)
cases.holding: Even though the US financed, armed, trained and planned for the contras, their acts were not attributable to it without effective control over the specific operations in which the violations occurred (para 115).
cases.use: The effective control test (Art 8).

cases.name: Prosecutor v Tadić (Appeals)
cases.holding: For organised armed groups, 'overall control' (financing, equipping, coordinating or helping plan military activity) suffices to make the group's acts those of the State, internationalising the conflict.
cases.use: The rival test, valid for conflict classification only.

cases.name: Bosnia v Serbia (Genocide)
cases.holding: The Srebrenica genocide was not attributable to Serbia: the VRS was not a de facto organ under complete dependence, and there was no effective control over the operation. Overall control was rejected for attribution. Serbia breached its duty to prevent, given its capacity to influence the Bosnian Serbs, and its duty to punish (failure to cooperate with the ICTY, Mladić).
cases.use: Arts 4 and 8; due diligence prevention; tests versus outcomes.

cases.name: US Diplomatic and Consular Staff in Tehran (US v Iran)
cases.holding: The militants' seizure of the embassy was not attributable to Iran, since they had not been charged with a specific operation by a competent organ; but Iran breached its own duties under the Vienna Conventions by failing to take any appropriate steps to protect the mission. Once Khomeini and other organs approved the occupation and decided to perpetuate it, the militants became agents of Iran (para 74). Diplomatic law is a 'self-contained regime' whose remedies (persona non grata, breaking relations) exclude reprisals against diplomats (paras 83–87).
cases.use: Non-attribution does not mean non-responsibility (due diligence); Art 11 adoption requires more than approval; why Art 50(2)(b) protects diplomatic inviolability.

cases.name: Caire (France v Mexico)
cases.holding: Mexico was responsible for the killing of a French national by two officers who acted outside their competence and against orders, because they acted under cover of their official status and used the means placed at their disposal by virtue of that status.
cases.use: Art 7 ARSIWA: ultra vires acts in an official capacity are attributable.

cards.q: What are the two elements of an internationally wrongful act?
cards.a: Conduct attributable to the State under international law, and a breach of an international obligation of that State (Art 2). Damage and fault aren't required unless the primary rule says so.

cards.q: Effective control versus overall control: which court, and which purpose?
cards.a: Effective control (ICJ, Nicaragua and Bosnia) is control over the specific operation, used for attribution under Art 8. Overall control (ICTY, Tadić) is general control over the group, used for classifying an armed conflict as international. The ICJ rejected overall control for attribution.

cards.q: When are private militants' acts attributable through Art 11?
cards.a: When the State acknowledges and adopts the conduct as its own, clearly and unequivocally, as Iran did in the Tehran Hostages case through official approval plus the decision to perpetuate the occupation (para 74). Approval alone is not enough.

cards.q: What are the cumulative necessity conditions in Art 25?
cards.a: The only way; an essential interest; grave and imminent peril; no serious impairment of the other State's or the community's essential interest. Barred if the obligation excludes necessity or the State contributed.

cards.q: Distress versus force majeure?
cards.a: Force majeure: performance is materially impossible because of an irresistible or unforeseen event, so the conduct is involuntary. Distress: there is a choice, but the only reasonable way to save the lives of the agent or persons in their care is to breach.

cards.q: If attribution fails, what is the fallback argument?
cards.a: Breach of the State's own positive obligation of due diligence (to prevent, protect or punish), measured by knowledge and capacity to influence (Corfu Channel; Bosnia Genocide para 430).

cards.q: What does Art 27 add?
cards.a: Invoking a circumstance precluding wrongfulness doesn't prejudice compliance once the circumstance ends, nor compensation for material loss.

cards.q: Complicity under Art 16 in Bosnia v Serbia: why wasn't Serbia complicit?
cards.a: Complicity requires at least knowledge of the principal's specific intent (dolus specialis). It was not established that Serbia supplied aid knowing the VRS intended genocide (paras 421–422). Art 16 also requires that the act would be wrongful if committed by the assisting State; the Court applied it by analogy to a non-State principal.

cards.q: Valdoria problem: is the beating of the engineers attributable?
cards.a: Ironwatch is not an organ (Art 4) and not empowered by law (Art 5). Under Art 8 there were no instructions and no effective control over the beating ('Do what you think best' concerns the convoy). Art 7 ultra vires applies only to organs or Art 5 entities. Art 11 fails: the Minister condemned it, and continued payment is not clear and unequivocal adoption. So it is likely not attributable, but argue Valdoria's own failure of due diligence.

cards.q: Tehran Hostages: how was Iran responsible in each phase?
cards.a: Phase one: the attack was not attributable (no specific instruction; general encouragement is not enough, paras 58–59), but Iran breached its own duty to protect the mission under VCDR Art 22(2) by doing nothing despite knowledge and means (paras 61–68). Phase two: approval plus the decision to perpetuate the occupation turned the militants into State agents (para 74; Art 11). Approval alone is not adoption.

cards.q: Necessity: which details from Gabčíkovo decide most cases?
cards.a: The conditions are cumulative and the State 'is not the sole judge' (para 51). 'Imminence' means 'immediacy or proximity', far beyond 'possibility'; a long-term peril counts only if 'certain and inevitable', and scientific uncertainty alone cannot establish a peril (para 54). Costlier alternatives still count as other means (para 55; CMS para 324). A State's own changes of course can amount to contribution (para 57). Wall AO para 140: the wall was not the only means.

cards.q: If fault is not required, why did Corfu Channel turn on Albania's knowledge?
cards.a: Because the primary rule required it: the obligation was not to allow one's territory to be used 'knowingly' for acts contrary to others' rights. ARSIWA is objective (Art 2 Commentary; Bosnia Genocide excluded fault from the general regime). Damage is not required either (Certain Activities/Construction of a Road, 2015). Separate regimes impose strict or absolute liability for harm (1972 Space Liability Convention; Trail Smelter).

cards.q: Justifications versus excuses: why does the label matter for compensation?
cards.a: Consent, self-defence and countermeasures make the act lawful (justifications). Force majeure, distress and necessity excuse conduct that remains wrongful (Paddeu, cited by Hernández), so compensation for material loss may still be owed (Art 27(b); Gabčíkovo para 48; CMS paras 388–394). A treaty emergency clause such as BIT Art XI is a primary rule: if it applies there is no breach and no Art 27(b) question (CMS annulment), which explains why LG&E put losses during the emergency on the investor.

cards.q: When is an ultra vires act of an official attributable?
cards.a: When the official acted in an official capacity, using the authority or means of the office, even against orders (Art 7; Caire, Youmans). A purely private act is not attributable (Mallén's off-duty assault), unless the State fails its own due-diligence duty. Art 7 applies only to organs (Art 4) and Art 5 entities, not to private persons under Art 8.

excerpts.source: ILC Articles on State Responsibility (2001)
excerpts.text: The conduct of a person or group of persons shall be considered an act of a State under international law if the person or group of persons is in fact acting on the instructions of, or under the direction or control of, that State in carrying out the conduct.
excerpts.why: Attribution of private conduct; 'control' read as effective control (Nicaragua, Bosnia).

excerpts.source: Nicaragua v US
excerpts.text: For this conduct to give rise to legal responsibility of the United States, it would in principle have to be proved that that State had effective control of the military or paramilitary operations in the course of which the alleged violations were committed.
excerpts.why: Effective control over the specific operations, not just financing, training and planning.

excerpts.source: Application of the Genocide Convention (Bosnia and Herzegovina v Serbia and Montenegro)
excerpts.text: …the 'overall control' test has the major drawback of broadening the scope of State responsibility well beyond the fundamental principle governing the law of international responsibility: a State is responsible only for its own conduct…
excerpts.why: The ICJ rejects Tadić's overall control for attribution; it may still serve for classifying conflicts.

topics.title: State responsibility II: consequences and invocation
core: Legal consequences (Part Two): the duty of performance continues (Art 29); cessation and, if circumstances require, assurances and guarantees of non-repetition (Art 30); full reparation for injury, material or moral (Art 31, Chorzów).

Forms of reparation, in this order: restitution, unless materially impossible or wholly disproportionate (Art 35); compensation for financially assessable damage, including loss of profits (Art 36); satisfaction, such as acknowledgment, regret, apology or a declaration, which must not be humiliating (Art 37). Contributory fault reduces reparation (Art 39).

Serious breaches of peremptory norms (Arts 40–41): all States must cooperate to end the breach through lawful means, must not recognise the situation as lawful, and must not render aid or assistance in maintaining it (see the 2004 Wall AO and the 2024 OPT AO).

Invocation by an injured State (Art 42): the obligation is owed to it individually; or it is owed to a group or the international community and the State is specially affected, or the obligation is 'integral' (breach affects all parties' performance, e.g. disarmament).

Invocation by non-injured States (Art 48): obligations erga omnes partes, protecting a collective interest of a group, or erga omnes, owed to the international community as a whole (Barcelona Traction para 33). They may claim cessation, guarantees, and reparation in the interest of the injured State or beneficiaries (Belgium v Senegal paras 68–70; Climate Change AO 2025 para 443). Gambia v Myanmar, Merits (19 Nov 2026, paras 585–590, 609–610, 621–625) applied this. The Gambia, though not injured, obtained guarantees of non-repetition, restitution and compensation for the Rohingya 'as a group and as individuals' (Myanmar's own population), without needing a mandate from them; it cannot claim reparation for itself. Compensation will be fixed by the ICJ in a later phase.
Admissibility (Art 44): nationality of claims rules (diplomatic protection) and exhaustion of local remedies. Loss of the right to invoke through waiver or acquiescence (Art 45).

Diplomatic protection (Mavrommatis): by taking up a national's claim, the State asserts its own right to ensure respect for international law in the person of its nationals. It is discretionary for the State.
Countermeasures (Arts 49–54) are taken only by an injured State, against the responsible State, to induce compliance. They must be temporary and as far as possible reversible.

Countermeasures must be proportionate, commensurate with the injury, taking into account the gravity of the wrong and the rights in question (Art 51; Gabčíkovo para 85; Air Service 'some degree of equivalence').

Procedure (Art 52): call on the State to comply, notify the decision and offer to negotiate, though urgent countermeasures are allowed. Suspend them if the wrong has ceased and the dispute is before a tribunal with binding powers.

Countermeasures may not affect (Art 50): the prohibition of force, fundamental human rights, humanitarian obligations prohibiting reprisals, jus cogens, or (Art 50(2)) dispute-settlement obligations in force with the target State and the inviolability of diplomatic or consular agents, premises, archives and documents.

Third-State countermeasures (Art 54) are left open ('lawful measures'). Contemporary practice, such as sanctions against Russia, adds weight, but they remain contested. Retorsion (unfriendly but lawful acts) is always allowed.

Remedies in practice. Restitution was ordered in Tehran Hostages (release, return of premises), Temple of Preah Vihear 1962 (return of objects) and Arrest Warrant 2002 para 76 (cancel the warrant), and refused in Pulp Mills 2010 (dismantling the mill was inappropriate for procedural breaches). Compensation: Corfu Channel (£843,947), Diallo 2012 (US$95,000, of which US$85,000 non-material), Certain Activities 2018 (the ICJ's first award for environmental damage), DRC v Uganda 2022 (US$325m in global sums). Compensation dominates in practice and the injured State may choose it (Art 43(2)(b)). Art 35 restores the situation before the act, not Chorzów's hypothetical situation; compensation covers the gap, such as lost profits. Interest is due where needed for full reparation (Art 38).

Jus cogens versus erga omnes: jus cogens concerns the rank of a norm (no derogation, VCLT Art 53); erga omnes concerns to whom the obligation is owed and so who has standing (Barcelona Traction paras 33–34). Every peremptory norm gives rise to erga omnes obligations (ILC 2022, Conclusion 17), but not necessarily the reverse. Arts 40–41 use the first concept, Art 48 the second. There are no 'State crimes': Ago's draft Art 19 (1976) was dropped by Crawford, there are no punitive damages, and obligations under the Genocide Convention 'are not of a criminal nature' (Bosnia Genocide para 170).

Standing is not jurisdiction: 'the erga omnes character of a norm and the rule of consent to jurisdiction are two different things' (East Timor 1995 para 29). Art 48 cases still rested on compromissory clauses (CAT Art 30; Genocide Convention Art IX). Several responsible States (Art 47): each may be held responsible, with no double recovery (Corfu Channel: Albania liable although another State probably laid the mines; Nauru 1992: Australia sued alone). The limit is Monetary Gold: no ruling where an absent State's interests form 'the very subject-matter of the decision'. Loss of the right to invoke (Art 45): no fixed time limit, and delay alone does not bar a claim (Nauru para 32).

Direct versus indirect injury: the Art 44 admissibility rules (nationality of claims, local remedies) apply only when a State claims for injury to its nationals. Direct injury to the State itself (e.g. an attack on its embassy) needs neither; mixed claims are judged by which element predominates (Avena 2004 para 40: Mexico claimed in its own name, so no exhaustion was required). An Art 48 claim needs no nationality link (Gambia v Myanmar 2022 para 109). The local remedies rule is customary (Interhandel 1959; ELSI 1989) and requires only available and effective remedies.

Diplomatic protection, the ILC Articles (2006) in detail: dual nationals may be protected against a third State by either State of nationality (Art 6), but against the other State of nationality only by the State of predominant nationality (Art 7; Mergé 1955; IUSCT Case A/18, 'dominant and effective' nationality). Stateless persons and refugees may be protected by the State of lawful and habitual residence (Art 8, progressive development). Companies are protected by the State of incorporation (Art 9; Barcelona Traction); shareholders only for direct injury to their own rights, or where the company has ceased to exist or had to incorporate in the wrongdoing State (Arts 11–12). 'Protection by substitution' is not custom (Diallo 2007 paras 86–94). Local remedies exceptions (Art 15): no reasonable possibility of effective redress, undue delay, no relevant connection, waiver. There is no individual right to protection in international law (Barcelona Traction paras 78–79), and domestic courts (Abbasi, UK 2002; Kaunda, South Africa 2004; Khadr, Canada 2010) have found none enforceable.

Countermeasures by non-injured States (Art 54), the record: the ILC Commentary listed six instances (US against Uganda 1978; Western States against Poland and the USSR 1981; the EC, Australia, Canada and NZ against Argentina 1982; the US against South Africa 1986; against Iraq 1990; the EC against the FRY 1998), found the practice 'sparse' and dropped its 2000 draft allowing collective countermeasures after objections in the Sixth Committee. 'Lawful measures' was chosen so as not to prejudge the answer. Since then the IDI Krakow Resolution (2005, Art 5(c)) accepts non-forcible countermeasures after a widely acknowledged grave breach of an erga omnes obligation, and Tams and Dawidowicz see a permissive rule. Alland's critique: States appoint themselves guardians of the community interest, and only powerful States can do so.
lecture: Art 30 illustrated: cessation (Rainbow Warrior) and guarantees of non-repetition (LaGrand).

Reparation requires injury plus causation, a 'sufficiently direct and certain causal nexus' (Bosnian Genocide: no compensation for the duty to prevent because it was not shown the genocide would have been averted).

Art 40: a serious breach is a gross or systematic failure to fulfil a peremptory obligation. Art 41 consequences in practice: the 2024 OPT AO (para 278) — no recognition of changes to the territory's character, composition or status since 1967; abstain from treaty relations concerning the OPT, from economic and trade dealings, and, in establishing and maintaining diplomatic missions in Israel, from any recognition of its illegal presence in the OPT.
Art 42 injured State: owed individually; or owed to a group or the community and the breach specially affects it or radically changes the position of all others (integral obligations).

Art 48 non-injured States: obligations erga omnes partes or erga omnes; may claim cessation, guarantees and reparation for the beneficiaries. Quoted: Gambia v Myanmar (Preliminary Objections 2022, para 108) — any State party may invoke responsibility for breaches of the Genocide Convention. Countermeasures to ensure cessation are left to Art 54.
Admissibility (Art 44): nationality of claims and exhaustion of local remedies, with diplomatic protection as an aside.

Countermeasures: otherwise wrongful acts, non-forcible (Art 50), aimed at inducing compliance (Art 49), described in the Commentaries as 'a feature of a decentralized system'. They cannot breach peremptory norms, fundamental human rights, humanitarian prohibitions of reprisals, dispute-settlement obligations, or diplomatic inviolability; they must be proportionate (Art 51) and follow procedure (Art 52).

Gambia v Myanmar, Merits 2026. The judgment cites the 2022 Preliminary Objections judgment at para 109 (common interest of all States parties) and para 112 ('any State party ... may invoke the responsibility of another State party, including through the institution of proceedings before the Court'); the lecture slide quotes the same reasoning from the 2022 judgment as para 108. It adds that Art IX jurisdiction extends to reparation (paras 579-580) and that erga omnes partes standing extends to guarantees of non-repetition and reparation in the interest of the beneficiaries (para 590).

cases.name: Mavrommatis Palestine Concessions (Greece v UK)
cases.holding: By taking up a national's case, a State asserts its own rights. It also defined a dispute as a disagreement on a point of law or fact, a conflict of legal views or interests.
cases.use: Diplomatic protection as the State's own right; the definition of a dispute.

cases.name: Air Service Agreement (US/France)
cases.holding: The US suspension of Air France flights to Los Angeles in response to France's breach of the bilateral agreement was a lawful countermeasure: proportionate, with 'some degree of equivalence', and countermeasures are not barred during negotiations.
cases.use: The leading countermeasures case: proportionality and the relation to negotiations.

cases.name: Obligation to Prosecute or Extradite (Belgium v Senegal)
cases.holding: CAT obligations are erga omnes partes. Every party has a common interest in compliance, so Belgium had standing without being specially affected. Senegal breached Arts 6(2) and 7(1) by failing to prosecute Habré or extradite him.
cases.use: Art 48 standing; aut dedere aut judicare.

cases.name: Rainbow Warrior (remedies)
cases.holding: Restitution was impossible because the obligation had expired. The public declaration of breach was appropriate satisfaction, and the tribunal recommended a fund for friendship between the two States.
cases.use: Satisfaction; the limits of restitution.

cases.name: Gabčíkovo-Nagymaros (countermeasures)
cases.holding: Variant C (diverting the Danube) was a response to Hungary's wrong but was disproportionate because it deprived Hungary of its right to an equitable share of a shared resource.
cases.use: Proportionality; the conditions for countermeasures.

cases.name: LaGrand (Germany v US)
cases.holding: The US breached the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations (Art 36). The Court accepted US assurances as a general guarantee of non-repetition and held that provisional measures are binding.
cases.use: Assurances and guarantees of non-repetition (Art 30(b)).

cases.name: The Gambia v Myanmar (Merits)
cases.holding: A non-injured State party may invoke Myanmar's responsibility and claim cessation, assurances and guarantees of non-repetition, and performance of the obligation of full reparation (restitution and compensation) in the interest of the Rohingya group and individual victims, based on Art 48(2) ARSIWA and Climate Change AO para 443. The State cannot claim reparation for itself (paras 585-590, 609-610).
cases.use: Art 48 remedies for erga omnes partes breaches; reparation to individuals or groups via an inter-State case; follows Belgium v Senegal and Preliminary Objections 2022.

cases.name: Naulilaa (Portugal v Germany)
cases.holding: Germany's 1914 attacks on Portuguese forts and posts in Angola, after three Germans were killed at Naulila, were an unlawful reprisal: there was no prior wrongful act (the deaths followed a misunderstanding), no prior demand for redress, and the force was out of all proportion.
cases.use: The classic conditions for reprisals (now countermeasures): prior wrong, prior demand, proportionality; armed reprisals are now prohibited (Art 50(1)(a); Res 2625).

cases.name: East Timor (Portugal v Australia)
cases.holding: Although the right of self-determination is erga omnes, the Court could not rule on Australia's conduct under the Timor Gap Treaty because doing so would require deciding on the lawfulness of Indonesia's conduct, and Indonesia had not consented to jurisdiction (Monetary Gold). 'The erga omnes character of a norm and the rule of consent to jurisdiction are two different things' (para 29).
cases.use: Standing under Art 48 does not create jurisdiction; the Monetary Gold limit in cases with several wrongdoers (Art 47).

cases.name: Ahmadou Sadio Diallo (Guinea v DRC), Compensation
cases.holding: Awarded Guinea US$95,000 for Mr Diallo's unlawful detention and expulsion, including US$85,000 for non-material injury; the sum was intended to repair Mr Diallo's own injury (para 57).
cases.use: Moral damage to individuals is compensable; modern diplomatic protection serving human rights.

cards.q: What are the forms of reparation, in order?
cards.a: Restitution (Art 35), compensation (Art 36), satisfaction (Art 37), applied singly or combined, with full reparation as the goal (Art 31). Contributory fault reduces it (Art 39).

cards.q: Art 42 versus Art 48: who may invoke, and what can they ask?
cards.a: Art 42, the injured State: all remedies, plus countermeasures. Art 48, any State for an erga omnes (partes) obligation: cessation, guarantees, and reparation in the interest of the injured or beneficiaries.

cards.q: What are the conditions for lawful countermeasures?
cards.a: A prior wrongful act by the target; taken by the injured State; aimed at inducing compliance; prior demand and notification with an offer to negotiate (Art 52); proportionate (Art 51); temporary and reversible; not affecting Art 50 obligations; suspended when the matter is before a binding tribunal and the wrong has ceased.

cards.q: Which obligations may never be affected by countermeasures?
cards.a: Refraining from the threat or use of force; fundamental human rights; humanitarian prohibitions of reprisals; other jus cogens (Art 50(1)); and, for the State taking them, obligations under dispute-settlement procedures in force with the target State and the inviolability of diplomatic or consular agents, premises, archives and documents (Art 50(2)).

cards.q: What are the third-State duties in Art 41 for serious breaches of jus cogens?
cards.a: Cooperate to end the breach through lawful means; do not recognise the resulting situation as lawful; do not render aid or assistance in maintaining it.

cards.q: What must a claimant satisfy for diplomatic protection?
cards.a: The nationality of claims: the injured person must be a national (Nottebohm's genuine-link test is contested and is not required by the ILC Articles on Diplomatic Protection 2006, Art 4 and commentary); continuous nationality (Art 5) and exhaustion of effective local remedies (Art 44 ARSIWA; ILC Articles on Diplomatic Protection).

cards.q: What did the 2024 OPT AO (para 278) require of third States?
cards.a: Not to recognise changes in the physical character, demographic composition, institutional structure or status of the territory occupied since 1967, and to abstain from treaty relations on behalf of the OPT, economic and trade dealings that entrench the occupation, and, in establishing and maintaining diplomatic missions in Israel, from any recognition of its illegal presence in the OPT; States must also take steps to prevent trade or investment relations that help maintain the illegal situation — Art 41 duties applied.

cards.q: Which causation standard governs reparation?
cards.a: A 'sufficiently direct and certain causal nexus' between the wrongful act and the injury (Bosnian Genocide para 462). Serbia's failure to prevent did not lead to compensation because it was not shown the genocide would have been averted; a declaration was satisfaction.

cards.q: Can a non-injured State obtain compensation for victims in an erga omnes partes case?
cards.a: Yes. In Gambia v Myanmar (Merits, 19 Nov 2026) the ICJ held that The Gambia may claim performance of the obligation of full reparation, including restitution and compensation, in the interest of the Rohingya as a group and as individuals, without a mandate, but not reparation for itself (paras 589-590, 609-610, 624). The amount and modalities will be decided later, after Myanmar reports within two years (para 625).

cards.q: Jus cogens or erga omnes: what is the difference and why does it matter in an answer?
cards.a: Jus cogens: the norm's rank, no derogation (VCLT 53), triggering Arts 26, 40–41 ARSIWA. Erga omnes: the obligation is owed to all (or to all treaty parties), so any State may invoke it under Art 48 (Barcelona Traction 33–34; Belgium v Senegal). All peremptory norms are erga omnes, not necessarily the reverse. Neither confers jurisdiction (DRC v Rwanda; East Timor para 29).

cards.q: Retorsion, countermeasure, suspension under VCLT Art 60, sanctions: how do they differ?
cards.a: Retorsion: lawful in itself, no prior breach needed (expelling diplomats, cutting aid). Countermeasure: otherwise unlawful, wrongfulness precluded (Art 22), answers any breach, temporary, outside Art 50. Art 60: needs a material breach of the same treaty and suspends or ends the treaty itself (Gabčíkovo para 106). Armed reprisals: prohibited. SC sanctions: Chapter VII, need a threat to the peace, not a breach. Interim Accord (2011): Greece pleaded both Art 60 and countermeasures and failed on both.

cards.q: Who bears the risk if a countermeasure rests on a mistaken view that the other State breached first?
cards.a: The acting State: it judges for itself, and if it is wrong its measure is simply a wrongful act (ILC Commentary to Art 49, para 3). Air Services: countermeasures should be 'a wager on the wisdom, not on the weakness of the other Party'; the right to start them disappears once a tribunal can act (paras 94–96), and the State must expedite the arbitration (para 98).

cards.q: Is moral damage repaired by compensation or by satisfaction?
cards.a: Non-material harm to individuals (suffering, distress) is compensable (Art 36 Commentary; Diallo 2012: US$85,000). Non-material injury to the State itself (insult to its dignity, a violation of sovereignty without material loss) is repaired by satisfaction (Art 37: acknowledgment, regret, apology, a declaration — Corfu Channel, Rainbow Warrior).

excerpts.source: Factory at Chorzów (Germany v Poland)
excerpts.text: …reparation must, as far as possible, wipe out all the consequences of the illegal act and re-establish the situation which would, in all probability, have existed if that act had not been committed.
excerpts.why: Full reparation (ARSIWA Art 31): restitution first, then compensation, then satisfaction.

excerpts.source: Barcelona Traction (Belgium v Spain)
excerpts.text: …an essential distinction should be drawn between the obligations of a State towards the international community as a whole, and those arising vis-à-vis another State in the field of diplomatic protection. By their very nature the former are the concern of all States. In view of the importance of the rights involved, all States can be held to have a legal interest in their protection; they are obligations erga omnes.
excerpts.why: The basis of ARSIWA Art 48 standing for non-injured States, applied in Gambia v Myanmar.

problems.title: Jalapenia and the Goldshell Crab
problems.source: Week 7 working-group questions (sample exam question, 25 points)
problems.prompt:
Save the Goldshell Crab (SGC), a Rustican action group, thinks Rustico is doing too little to stop Jalapenia fishing the endangered Goldshell Crab. From April 2018 it holds marches in Rustico's capital, Daim, which turn violent: on 10 May protesters smash shop windows and throw fireworks at the police; on 1 June a crowd storms the parliament building, leaving 5 dead and 150 injured, before the police restore order and make arrests.

On 5 September 2018 eight Jalapenian fishing boats on the Rio del Oro are blown up. In a YouTube video the SGC's leader, 'General Rainbow', claims the attack as a warning and threatens much worse if Jalapenia keeps fishing the crab, boasting that the group has enough explosives to destroy a whole city.

You advise Jalapenia's Ministry of Defence. May Jalapenia lawfully act in self-defence? Assess every condition.
issues: Frame: Art 2(4) and the Art 51 exception; self-defence is also customary (Nicaragua).

Armed attack: is the destruction of eight fishing boats grave enough in scale and effects (Nicaragua para 191; Oil Platforms para 72: the Court did not exclude that the mining of a single military vessel might suffice)? Are fishing boats 'State' targets or private property?

Author: the SGC is a non-state actor. Attribution to Rustico (Art 8 ARSIWA effective control; Res 3314 Art 3(g) 'sent by or on behalf of', 'substantial involvement')? The facts show discontent with, not support from, Rustico.

Self-defence against non-state actors: Wall para 139 and DRC v Uganda paras 146–147 (restrictive) versus post-9/11 practice and SC Res 1368/1373 and 'unwilling or unable'. Is Rustico unwilling or unable (it regained control of parliament and made arrests)?
The threat to 'destroy an entire city': anticipatory self-defence against an imminent attack (Caroline) versus a pre-emptive response to a non-imminent threat; conditional threat ('if anyone dares').
Necessity: are there alternatives (cooperation with Rustico's police, which has shown capacity)? Proportionality of any response; reporting to the SC.

Conclusion: very likely no right to use force on Rustican territory; Jalapenia may act on its own territory and waters, ask Rustico to prevent attacks (Corfu Channel due diligence) and invoke Rustico's responsibility if it fails.

problems.title: Assad at Tegel Airport
problems.prompt:
On 10 January 2019 German police arrest Syria's sitting President, Bashar al-Assad, at Berlin's Tegel Airport during a private visit to relatives, on a warrant from the Federal Prosecutor General. Germany wants to try him under its Code of Crimes against International Law (VStGB) for war crimes, crimes against humanity and torture committed in Syria between 2013 and 2018 by Syrian troops against about 2,000 Syrian, 400 French and 10 German nationals. He allegedly ordered attacks on civilians, the use of chemical weapons and the abuse of detainees. The Prosecutor also points to German interests, citing the costs of the refugee influx. The defence argues that a serving Head of State cannot be tried by a foreign national court, and that Germany lacks jurisdiction because the crimes took place abroad and few victims were German.

(1) On which jurisdictional bases could Germany rely, and which fail? (2) Is the immunity objection right, and what else could block a German prosecution? (3) Would the answer change if he came to Germany six months after leaving office? (4) What if, still in office, he were arrested in the Netherlands on an ICC warrant after a Security Council referral of Syria, a non-party?
issues: Jurisdiction: universal jurisdiction (custom for war crimes and CAH; CAT Arts 5(2), 6, 7 since he is present); passive personality (10 German victims). Not territoriality, not active nationality. The protective principle fails: refugee costs are not a vital State interest attacked by the conduct.

Sitting Head of State: immunity ratione personae is absolute before foreign national courts, including for international crimes (Arrest Warrant paras 51–61); arrest violates inviolability. Germany must release him.

After stepping down: personal immunity ends; functional immunity for official acts. Argue no functional immunity for torture (Pinochet; CAT logic) and possibly for core crimes (ILC draft Art 7, contested). Arrest Warrant para 61 avenue: acts 'in a private capacity' versus the trend to deny functional immunity for international crimes.

ICC route: Art 27 removes official capacity. SC referral under Art 13(b) binds Syria to cooperate as if a party (Al-Bashir Jordan Appeal 2019: no customary head-of-State immunity vis-à-vis international courts). The Netherlands must arrest and surrender (Art 89); Art 98(1) tension; Mongolia/Putin non-compliance finding (2024) as a contrast.
Structure: one heading per sub-question, rule then application, short conclusion each.

problems.title: EU 'friendly nations' raw materials
problems.prompt:
To cut its reliance on critical raw materials and rare earths from countries it sees as a security risk, the EU gives preference to imports from 'friendly nations' on a Commission list, which pay lower tariffs on these goods. Imports from China, judged especially risky, remain possible but only within quotas the Commission revises by regulation every six months. China starts WTO dispute settlement.

With reference to the GATT: (a) which claims can China bring under the core WTO obligations? (b) Can the EU justify its measures?
issues: Forum: compulsory and exclusive WTO jurisdiction (DSU Arts 6.1, 23.1); Appellate Body paralysis (appeal into the void; MPIA).
MFN (Art I:1): an advantage (lower tariff) granted to some members' like products is not extended 'immediately and unconditionally' to all, including China.
Tariff bindings (Art II) if rates exceed bound levels for China.
Quantitative restrictions (Art XI:1) on Chinese imports; non-discriminatory administration of quotas (Art XIII).

Defence under Art XXI(b)(iii): 'emergency in international relations' is objectively reviewable (Russia – Traffic in Transit); is economic dependence an emergency? Good faith and minimum plausibility linking measures to security interests; 'which it considers' covers the necessity of the measures and the Member's definition of its own essential security interests (both subject to good faith and minimum plausibility), but not the objective circumstances listed in (i)-(iii).

Defence under Art XX: (g) exhaustible natural resources needs even-handed domestic restrictions; (j) short supply; (b) unlikely. Then the chapeau: a political 'friends' list risks arbitrary or unjustifiable discrimination (US – Shrimp).
Other exceptions do not fit: Art XXIV covers customs unions and FTAs, not a Commission list. Conclusion: strong prima facie violations; the security exception is the EU's best but uncertain defence.

problems.title: Valdoria, Ironwatch and the Karsk Plateau
problems.prompt:
Valdoria and Estoria dispute the mineral-rich Karsk Plateau; both are parties to the VCDR and the ICCPR. In January, Valdoria's defence ministry signs up Ironwatch Ltd, a private Valdorian security firm: Valdoria supplies arms, fuel, satellite intelligence and a monthly fee, and Ironwatch is to help defend Valdorian interests on the Plateau, with no instructions on specific operations. The defence minister says publicly that Valdoria does not control Ironwatch and only supports 'patriots'.

In March a Valdorian intelligence officer sends Ironwatch's commander, Brandt, a satellite image of an Estorian mining convoy, noting that it is vulnerable and that he should do as he sees fit. Brandt's unit stops the convoy, destroys its equipment and holds eleven Estorian engineers for three weeks in an old barracks without consular access. Brandt has two engineers beaten for refusing to hand over geological data. Valdorian officials did not know; the minister condemned it on finding out, but Ironwatch's fee kept being paid.

In April the Karsk Liberation Front (KLF), a nominally independent militia that Valdoria has trained, armed and funded for years without ever directing its operations, attacks an Estorian border post.

Valdoria denies that any Ironwatch or KLF conduct is attributable to it and adds that the convoy was an unlawful armed incursion, so its response was self-defence. Estoria goes to the ICJ. Advise Estoria: (1) are (a) the detention and the destruction of the convoy, (b) the beatings and (c) the KLF attack attributable to Valdoria under ARSIWA? (2) Can Valdoria rely on a circumstance precluding wrongfulness for destroying the convoy?
issues: (a) Convoy: Ironwatch is not a de jure organ; de facto organ requires complete dependence (Nicaragua para 109; Bosnia para 392) — unlikely. Art 5: 'assist in the defence of Valdorian interests' is not empowerment by law to exercise governmental authority. Art 8: the intelligence officer's image plus 'Do what you think best' is arguably direction for this specific operation; argue instructions or direction, or effective control over the operation (Nicaragua para 115; Bosnia para 400). The Minister's denial of control is not decisive.

(b) Beating: outside any instruction; Art 7 ultra vires covers only organs and Art 5 entities, so a private actor's excess under Art 8 is attributable only if incidental to the instructed operation (ILC Commentary to Art 8 para 8). Art 11: condemnation, so no adoption; continuing the retainer is not clear and unequivocal acknowledgment. Fallback: Valdoria's own due diligence and ICCPR Art 7 and 9 duties; consular access (VCCR Art 36, not the VCDR named in the facts).

(c) KLF: years of arming and funding but no direction, so no effective control (Nicaragua); Tadić overall control rejected for attribution (Bosnia paras 403–406). Not attributable; but supply may itself breach the non-use of force and non-intervention (Nicaragua para 228).

(2) Self-defence (Art 21): requires an armed attack by Estoria; a mining convoy is not an armed attack in scale and effects, and response must be necessary and proportionate. Countermeasures (Art 22): require a prior wrong, notification, proportionality, non-forcible; destruction and detention fail. Necessity (Art 25) fails too.
Consequences: cessation, release, reparation (Arts 30–31; Chorzów); jurisdiction basis before the ICJ.

problems.title: Azargh's independence
problems.source: Week 2 working-group sample question, with the official model answer (20 points)
problems.prompt:
Azargh, a mountain region in southern Erebor, is mostly inhabited by ethnic Belerians, the people of neighbouring Beleria. Erebor claims it by historic title; Beleria relies on the self-determination of Azargh's population, which said it wanted to join Beleria in the late 1980s and declared independence in 1991. Only Beleria recognises the de facto Republic of Azargh.

As legal adviser to Azargh's foreign ministry, and citing authority: what does the right to self-determination mean for the people of Azargh and their aim of becoming an independent State? (20 points)
issues: OFFICIAL KEY (~5 pts) legal basis and peoples: self-determination in common Art 1 ICESCR/ICCPR — the right of a people to determine its political status (2); no definition of 'peoples' in IL (1); Azargh's population is ethnically distinct from Erebor's majority, a foundation for a 'people' claim (2).

OFFICIAL KEY (~5 pts) case law and external versus internal: being a people does not imply a right to an independent State (1); internal versus external self-determination, external including independence (Res 1541; Friendly Relations Declaration) (2); external self-determination accrues to colonial peoples and peoples under foreign subjugation (Res 1541, 2625; Kosovo and Chagos AOs) (2).

OFFICIAL KEY (~3 pts) uti possidetis and consent: outside those situations self-determination is at odds with uti possidetis and the integrity of borders (2); a declaration of independence like Azargh's in 1991 does not violate IL (Kosovo) (2); but to take effect, uti possidetis requires the consent of the parent State (Badinter) (2).

OFFICIAL KEY (~7 pts) application and conclusion: Azargh has a right to internal self-determination but can only establish an independent State with Erebor's consent (2). Extra points (up to the cap) for discussing remedial secession.

Useful extras: recognition only by Beleria (an interested neighbour) may be premature and evidences lack of statehood; effective government and independence from Beleria (puppet-State risk); joining Beleria instead raises territorial integrity and the prohibition on acquiring territory by force.

problems.title: Rio del Oro and the Goldshell Crab
problems.prompt:
Rustico and Jalapenia, neighbouring UN members (Koyoma is a third UN member), share the Rio del Oro, once rich in gold. Their 1885 Treaty of Friendship, Commerce and Navigation makes the thalweg the line for gold exploration. Article 1 commits them to exploit the river's 'exhaustible natural resources, including gold' equitably, and bars each from exploiting those resources beyond its thalweg.

By the 2010s the gold is mostly gone, but Jalapenia now fishes the Goldshell Crab, which lives on the riverbed, intensively across the whole river. The crab faces extinction and has been on CITES Appendix I since 2015, which bars commercial trade in wild specimens; all three States are CITES parties. After talks fail, Rustico sues Jalapenia at the ICJ in 2018 (jurisdiction is accepted) for breach of Article 1. Jalapenia says the crab falls outside it.

As clerk to an ICJ judge, using texts, literature and case law: does Article 1 cover fishing the crab, and how is the case likely to end for Jalapenia? Consider both sides' arguments. (30 points)
issues: Applicable rules: VCLT Arts 31–32 as custom for an 1885 treaty (Art 4 non-retroactivity; Costa Rica v Nicaragua para 47–48 applied them to an 1858 treaty). No restrictive interpretation in favour of sovereignty (para 48).

Ordinary meaning: 'exhaustible natural resources, including gold' — 'including' signals a non-exhaustive list; are living resources 'exhaustible'? Jalapenia: in 1885 the parties meant minerals (contemporaneity; 'exploit' and 'exploration' context); Rustico: generic term.
Context and object and purpose: equitable management of the river's resources between two States; the thalweg as a dividing line; title 'Friendship, Commerce and Navigation'.

Evolutive interpretation: Costa Rica v Nicaragua para 66 — generic terms in a treaty of long or unlimited duration are presumed to evolve; US – Shrimp (AB 1998): 'exhaustible natural resources' in GATT XX(g) covers living species, read with CITES; Art 31(3)(c) relevant rules (CITES Appendix I listing binding both parties) — systemic integration. Pauwelyn and Elsig on the ICJ sitting 'in between' textual and evolutive approaches.
Counter-arguments: Ukraine v Russia (2024) shows a narrower textual reading; Aegean Sea ('territorial status' evolving) supports Rustico.

Likely outcome: Article 1 applies to the Goldshell Crab, so Jalapenia's fishing beyond the thalweg breaches the treaty; remedies: cessation, possibly reparation. As clerk, weigh both sides neutrally and predict.

problems.title: The Varnia border strikes
problems.prompt: Varnia and Ostrel are UN members and parties to the ICJ Statute, and both have accepted compulsory jurisdiction under Art 36(2) without reservations. For two years the Liberation Front of Eastern Ostrel (LFEO), an armed separatist group, has operated from camps in northern Varnia. Varnia's intelligence service paid LFEO salaries, provided rifles and drones, and a Varnian colonel sat on the LFEO 'strategic council', which sets annual objectives. In March, LFEO fighters crossed into Ostrel and shelled a town, killing 40 civilians. Varnia's President praised the attack on television as 'a legitimate act of liberation that Varnia fully stands behind'. Two weeks later Ostrel launched air strikes on LFEO camps and on a Varnian army depot 50 km from the border, without reporting to the Security Council. Ostrel also froze the assets of Varnia's central bank and suspended the bilateral air services treaty. Varnia says the strikes were aggression and that Ostrel must pay compensation. Advise Ostrel.
issues: Did the LFEO attack amount to an armed attack? Consider scale and effects (Nicaragua), and whether one incident or an accumulation (Oil Platforms).

Attribution of LFEO conduct to Varnia: Art 4 de facto organ (complete dependence? likely not); Art 8 effective control over the March operation (the colonel on the strategic council suggests general, not operation-specific, control; Tadić overall control is not the ICJ test); Art 11 acknowledgment and adoption by the President's statement ('fully stands behind', compare Tehran Hostages).
Indirect armed attack through Res 3314 Art 3(g): 'sending' or 'substantial involvement'. Is the support enough under Nicaragua?

If not attributable, can Ostrel act in self-defence against a non-state actor on Varnian territory? Wall para 139 and DRC v Uganda versus the 'unwilling or unable' practice. Varnia's due diligence breach (Corfu Channel).
Necessity and proportionality: camps versus the depot 50 km away. Did the depot contribute to the attack (Oil Platforms target analysis)?
The failure to report under Art 51: not fatal, but evidential weight (Nicaragua para 200).
Asset freeze and treaty suspension as countermeasures: a prior wrong by Varnia; proportionality; Art 52 procedure; the central bank's immunity from execution; Air Service.
Remedies and forum: Art 36(2) jurisdiction; Varnia's counterclaims; reparation (Arts 31–37).

problems.title: The minister in Kelland
problems.prompt: General Dorn was Minister of Defence of Azeria until January. During his tenure Azerian forces tortured detainees from the Mirani minority, some of them nationals of Kelland. In February Dorn became Azeria's Foreign Minister. In June, while on an official visit to Kelland for a climate conference, he was arrested on a warrant issued by a Kellandic investigating judge for torture and crimes against humanity, based on Kelland's universal jurisdiction law and the Kellandic nationality of several victims. Separately, Mirani survivors are suing Azeria in Kelland's civil courts for damages, and the court has ordered the seizure of an Azerian State-owned airline's aircraft at Kelland airport. Kelland and Azeria are parties to the CAT. Azeria demands Dorn's immediate release and the lifting of the seizure. Advise Kelland.
issues: Bases of prescriptive jurisdiction: universal jurisdiction (CAT Arts 5 and 7; custom for CAH); passive personality (Kellandic victims); the presence of the accused at the time of arrest; Lotus versus the requirement of a permissive basis.

Immunity ratione personae of the incumbent Foreign Minister: Arrest Warrant applies directly. There is no exception for international crimes before foreign national courts, and arrest violates inviolability.
Acts done as Defence Minister: functional immunity would matter after office (Pinochet; ILC Draft Art 7), but now personal immunity bars everything.
Arrest Warrant para 61 alternatives: prosecution in Azeria, waiver, after office, international courts (ICC if it has jurisdiction, Art 27).
Civil claims against Azeria: State immunity for acta jure imperii (torture by armed forces); Germany v Italy; Al-Adsani; the territorial tort exception doesn't apply (acts in Azeria).

Seizure of the airline aircraft: immunity from execution is separate and stricter. Property must be in commercial use and connected to the entity (UN Convention Arts 19–21). Is a State-owned airline a separate entity?
Consequences: release, cessation, possible satisfaction; Kelland's obligations under CAT Art 7 (aut dedere aut judicare, Belgium v Senegal) versus immunity.

problems.title: Drought, a dam and a trade ban
problems.prompt: Under a 1995 treaty, Lacoria must release 40% of the River Sel's flow to downstream Brava. In 2026 an extreme drought, partly worsened by Lacoria's own decade of excessive irrigation, threatened Lacoria's capital with water shortages. Lacoria cut releases to 10% for eight months. Brava's farmers lost their harvest. In response, Brava (a) banned imports of all Lacorian agricultural products, claiming they are produced with water 'stolen' from Brava, and (b) refused to repay a sovereign loan instalment owed to Lacoria. Both are WTO members. Brava says Lacoria must restore the flow and pay for the lost harvest; Lacoria says it acted out of necessity and that Brava's ban violates the GATT. Advise both sides briefly, then give your view.
issues: Breach: reduced releases are a breach of the treaty obligation, attributable as State organ conduct (Art 4).

Necessity (Art 25): an essential interest (the capital's water supply) and grave and imminent peril (likely met). 'Only way'? (alternatives such as rationing and other sources). No serious impairment of Brava's essential interest? Contribution through irrigation (Gabčíkovo; CMS). It probably fails because of contribution.
Force majeure (Art 23)? The drought is an external event, but performance wasn't materially impossible and Lacoria contributed.
Art 27: compensation even if necessity succeeded; the duty to resume releases.
Reparation: cessation and restitution of flow; compensation for lost harvest (Art 36, Chorzów); contributory fault arguments (Art 39).

Brava's import ban: GATT Art XI violation; Art XX(b) or (g) (water as an exhaustible resource? the nexus); the chapeau; a ban on all products is over-broad. Can trade measures be countermeasures within the WTO (exclusive DSU, Art 23 DSU)?
Refusal to repay the loan as a countermeasure: a prior wrong; proportionality; reversibility; Art 52 notification; Air Service.

problems.title: Standing for the Rokai
problems.prompt: Security forces in Tessia are carrying out mass killings and forced deportations of the Rokai, an ethnic minority. A UN fact-finding mission finds 'reasonable grounds' that genocidal intent may be present. Delmar, a small State with no Rokai nationals and no ties to Tessia, wants to bring a case before the ICJ under the Genocide Convention (both are parties, and Tessia has no reservation to Art IX). Delmar also wants to impose a ban on Tessian State officials' assets and suspend a bilateral investment treaty with Tessia. Advise Delmar on (1) its standing and what it can ask for, and (2) whether its unilateral measures are lawful.
issues: Erga omnes partes obligations under the Genocide Convention (prevent and punish), and the common interest of all parties: Belgium v Senegal; Gambia v Myanmar.
Art 48 ARSIWA: a non-injured State may claim cessation, assurances, and reparation in the interest of the beneficiaries (the Rokai).
Provisional measures: plausibility of rights, urgency, irreparable harm (Gambia v Myanmar; South Africa v Israel).
Serious breach of a peremptory norm (Arts 40–41): duties of non-recognition, non-assistance, and cooperation to end it.
Asset ban on officials: may be retorsion if lawful in itself; check the immunity of officials' and State property.

BIT suspension as a third-State countermeasure: Art 54 ('lawful measures') and the debate (State practice on Russia sanctions); Art 50 limits; proportionality; alternatively treaty suspension under VCLT Art 60(1)-(2) for material breach? (Not applicable: Art 60 only covers breach of the same treaty, and the breach is of the Genocide Convention, not the BIT. Art 60(5) is the separate rule that humanitarian provisions may not be suspended.)

problems.title: The Republic of Esmera and the Lake Varo treaty
problems.prompt: In 2019 the eastern province of the State of Moria declared independence as the Republic of Esmera after a referendum boycotted by the non-Esmeran minority. Neighbouring Tarsis, whose troops had entered the province weeks before the referendum 'to protect ethnic Tarsians', recognised Esmera immediately; eleven other States followed by 2024. Esmera has a functioning administration, but its budget, currency and border security depend on Tarsis. In 2021 Esmera's Deputy Minister of Water signed a 'Memorandum on Lake Varo' with Moria's Ministry of Environment, under which each side 'shall' limit irrigation withdrawals to 30% of inflow; it states it 'enters into force upon signature' and was registered by Moria with the UN Secretariat. Esmera's constitution requires parliamentary approval for international agreements, which was never sought, and Esmera never protested the registration. In 2023 Esmera acceded to the 1997 UN Watercourses Convention with a reservation 'excluding Article 7 (no significant harm) in its entirety'; Moria objected but did not oppose the Convention's entry into force between them. In 2025, during a drought, Esmera tripled withdrawals and announced it was 'terminating' the Memorandum because of 'a fundamental change in climatic circumstances'. Moria asks whether Esmera is bound and has breached its obligations. Advise Moria.
issues: Is Esmera a State? Montevideo criteria; effective government versus dependence on Tarsis (independence; puppet-State analogies: Manchukuo, TRNC); legality — creation linked to Tarsis's use of force and a contested referendum (SC Res 541 TRNC analogy; Kosovo para 81); recognition by 12 States is evidence only (declaratory theory); Tarsis's recognition possibly premature and unlawful intervention. Consequence: if not a State, the Memorandum may not be a treaty under the VCLT (but could still bind as an agreement governed by IL with a limited subject).

Self-determination: are Esmerans a 'people' entitled to external self-determination? Not colonial or occupied; internal self-determination; Badinter and Quebec require parent consent; remedial secession contested.
If a State: is the Memorandum a treaty? Form and intent ('shall', entry into force on signature, registration, no protest — Qatar v Bahrain; Somalia v Kenya).

Authority (Art 7): a deputy minister lacks ex officio capacity — full powers? Subsequent confirmation (Art 8). Internal law: parliamentary approval not sought — Art 46 only if manifest and fundamental (Cameroon v Nigeria; Somalia v Kenya); acquiescence (Art 45).

Reservation excluding Art 7 of the Watercourses Convention: compatible with object and purpose (Art 19(c))? Effects of Moria's simple objection (Art 21(3)); an invalid reservation (ILC Guide 4.5.3). And the no-harm rule exists in custom anyway (Guide 4.4.2; Pulp Mills; Climate AO due diligence).

Termination for fundamental change (Art 62): drought foreseeable? essential basis? radical transformation? Gabčíkovo para 104 sets a very high bar; procedure (Arts 65–67) not followed. Necessity does not terminate (Gabčíkovo).

Breach and remedies: tripling withdrawals breaches the 30% cap; State responsibility; possible necessity defence (Art 25) fails if Esmera contributed or other means existed; Moria may claim cessation and reparation, consider countermeasures, and seize the ICJ if jurisdiction exists.
